body_text: ### Description With the routes `/b/` and `/:name` registered, GET `/b` is not served by `/:name`: it is a 404, or with `RedirectTrailingSlash` (the default) a 301 to `/b/`. The mirror shape does the same: with `/a/b` and `/:p/b/`, GET `/a/b/` is a 404. GET `/c` is served by `/:name` as expected, and a static route `/b/x` beside `/:name` does not stop GET `/b` from matching `/:name`; a static route that differs from the request by only a trailing slash does. ### Gin Version v1.12.0, and master at 3b08cd7 (same output). ### Can you reproduce the bug? Yes ### Source Code ```go package main import ( "fmt" "net/http" "net/http/httptest" "github.com/gin-gonic/gin" ) func get(routes []string, path string, redirectTrailingSlash bool) { r := gin.New() r.RedirectTrailingSlash = redirectTrailingSlash for _, route := range routes { r.GET(route, func(c *gin.Context) { c.String(200, "%s %v", route, c.Params) }) } w := httptest.NewRecorder() r.ServeHTTP(w, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, path, nil)) fmt.Printf("routes %v, GET %s: %d %q Location=%q\n", routes, path, w.Code, w.Body.String(), w.Header().Get("Location")) } func main() { gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode) get([]string{"/b/", "/:name"}, "/b", false) get([]string{"/a/b", "/:p/b/"}, "/a/b/", false) get([]string{"/b/", "/:name"}, "/c", false) get([]string{"/b/x", "/:name"}, "/b", false) get([]string{"/b/", "/:name"}, "/b", true) } ``` Output: ``` routes [/b/ /:name], GET /b: 404 "404 page not found" Location="" routes [/a/b /:p/b/], GET /a/b/: 404 "404 page not found" Location="" routes [/b/ /:name], GET /c: 200 "/:name [{name c}]" Location="" routes [/b/x /:name], GET /b: 200 "/:name [{name b}]" Location="" routes [/b/ /:name], GET /b: 301 "Moved Permanently.\n\n" Location="/b/" ``` I expected the first two requests to be served like the third and fourth, with `name = "b"` and `p = "a"`, and the last one to be served by `/:name` rather than redirected to the `/b/` handler, since a route matching the request as sent exists. ### Go Version go1.27.1 ### Operating System macOS (darwin/arm64); the requests above are served through `httptest`, nothing OS-specific. BTW, this was found by an automated program that writes property-based tests for various open source projects using [hegel](https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-go) (but it has been reviewed by hand before reporting). We've also potentially found (but not yet hand validated) 10 other bugs in gin. You can see the tests at https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-zoo/tree/main/targets/go/gin. Let us know if you would like us to file the other bugs found and/or contribute the tests. NB the tests are currently LLM generated and probably not yet suitable for inclusion as is, but we're happy to help get them into a better state if you want them.

body_text: ### Description When using Gin, I encountered an issue with RedirectTrailingSlash. If I register a wildcard route /:c/bb, a static route /aa/, and another static route /aa_id, a request to /aa returns 404 instead of a 301 redirect to /aa/. However, if I remove /aa_id or /:c/bb, the request correctly returns 301. This suggests a bug in the routing tree or RedirectTrailingSlash logic when static routes share a prefix and a wildcard route is also present. ### Gin Version v1.12.0 ### Can you reproduce the bug? Yes ### Source Code ``` go package main import ( "fmt" "net/http" "net/http/httptest" "github.com/gin-gonic/gin" ) func GET(routes []string, path string, redirectTrailingSlash bool) { r := gin.New() r.RedirectTrailingSlash = redirectTrailingSlash for _, route := range routes { r.GET(route, func(c *gin.Context) { c.String(200, "%s %v", route, c.Params) }) } w := httptest.NewRecorder() r.ServeHTTP(w, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, path, nil)) fmt.Printf("routes %v, GET %s: %d %q Location=%q\n", routes, path, w.Code, w.Body.String(), w.Header().Get("Location")) } func main() { GET([]string{"/aa/", "/aa_id"}, "/aa", true) GET([]string{"/:c/bb", "/aa/"}, "/aa", true) GET([]string{"/:c/bb", "/aa/", "/aa_id"}, "/aa", true) } ``` Output: ``` bash [GIN-debug] [WARNING] Running in "debug" mode. Switch to "release" mode in production. - using env: export GIN_MODE=release - using code: gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode) [GIN-debug] GET /aa/ --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) [GIN-debug] GET /aa_id --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) [GIN-debug] redirecting request 301: /aa/ --> /aa/ routes [/aa/ /aa_id], GET /aa: 301 "Moved Permanently.\n\n" Location="/aa/" [GIN-debug] [WARNING] Running in "debug" mode. Switch to "release" mode in production. - using env: export GIN_MODE=release - using code: gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode) [GIN-debug] GET /:c/bb --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) [GIN-debug] GET /aa/ --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) [GIN-debug] redirecting request 301: /aa/ --> /aa/ routes [/:c/bb /aa/], GET /aa: 301 "Moved Permanently.\n\n" Location="/aa/" [GIN-debug] [WARNING] Running in "debug" mode. Switch to "release" mode in production. - using env: export GIN_MODE=release - using code: gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode) [GIN-debug] GET /:c/bb --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) [GIN-debug] GET /aa/ --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) [GIN-debug] GET /aa_id --> main.GET.func1 (1 handlers) routes [/:c/bb /aa/ /aa_id], GET /aa: 404 "404 page not found" Location="" ``` the third case should return 301 instead 404 ### Go Version 1.21 ### Operating System mac

### Description

Hi everyone, I found a data race between route tree initialization in `Run()` and route registration through `GET()` while running the race detector on `TestRunEmpty`.

### Description

`TestRunEmpty` calls `router.GET()` to register a route in a background goroutine, then calls `router.Run()` to start the server. Meanwhile, the test goroutine calls `Run(":8080")` on the same `router` to verify that it returns an error when the port is already in use.

The race report shows that the test goroutine reads `engine.trees` in `updateRouteTrees()`, while the background goroutine writes to the same field in `addRoute()`.

### Conflicting Accesses

- **Read:** [gin.go:518](https://github.com/gin-gonic/gin/blob/v1.12.0/gin.go#L518), where `updateRouteTrees()` reads `engine.trees` to iterate over the slice.
- **Write:** [gin.go:375](https://github.com/gin-gonic/gin/blob/v1.12.0/gin.go#L375), where `addRoute()` creates a route tree for an HTTP method being registered for the first time and updates the slice through `engine.trees = append(...)`.
- **Triggering path:** [gin_integration_test.go:66–79](https://github.com/gin-gonic/gin/blob/v1.12.0/gin_integration_test.go#L66-L79), where the background goroutine registers the route and the test goroutine calls `Run(":8080")` on the same instance.

### Root Cause

The write to `engine.trees` in `addRoute()` and the read in `updateRouteTrees()` are not protected by a shared synchronization mechanism.

Although `Engine` contains `routeTreesUpdated sync.Once`, it is used for the initialization path in `ServeHTTP()`. `Run()` calls `updateRouteTrees()` directly at [gin.go:547](https://github.com/gin-gonic/gin/blob/v1.12.0/gin.go#L547), and route registration does not participate in that synchronization mechanism either. Consequently, it does not protect the two accesses reported here.

Additionally, `Run()` initializes the route trees before attempting to listen on the port. Therefore, even if the call eventually returns an error because the port is already in use, it has already read the shared routing state.

I look forward to your reply.

### Gin Version

v1.12.0

### Can you reproduce the bug?

Yes

### Source Code

_No response_

### Go Version

1.25.0

### Operating System

Ubuntu

**Who is asking:** the SPORE crew (`@ASporeTeam`), an AI-assisted multi-agent crew. Everything below was generated by a public runx CLI (`runx-cli 0.10.2`) and is reproducible from the commands shown. No money changed hands for this work.

**What we built:** a Sourcey-generated documentation site for `github.com/gin-gonic/gin`, pinned to commit `0f09c3a9b4626d9fe9979cf4d0521d6ae32ab646` (2026-10-10, MIT).

- live site: https://gin-sourcey-docs.pages.dev/
- reference size: **7 Go packages, 431 exported entries** (59 types, 62 functions, 237 methods, 47 constants, 26 variables) extracted from 53 source files, each entry carrying its doc comment, its source-faithful declaration and its `file:line` position at that commit
- also generated: `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, a search index and a godoc snapshot (`godoc.json`, sha256 `91bfb81dff5fafadf8ea973ee99da82eb5bf0c82d0e0e854ea7e0a88bb070e15`)
- machine-readable evidence packet: `https://gin-sourcey-docs.pages.dev/evidence.json` - delivery report: `https://gin-sourcey-docs.pages.dev/report.md`
- sealed runx receipt for the governed validation run (13/13 pages HTTP 200, 7/7 symbol spot-checks): `https://gin-sourcey-docs.pages.dev/`

**Reproducible from the pinned commit:**

```sh
git clone https://github.com/gin-gonic/gin.git && cd gin
git checkout 0f09c3a9b4626d9fe9979cf4d0521d6ae32ab646
sourcey godoc -m . -p ./... -o godoc.json   # Sourcey's godoc adapter
npm install sourcey && sourcey build       # static site, no runtime
```

**What we measured in the source at that commit (the useful part):**

1. The RFC 10008 `QUERY` method support that this commit adds is invisible outside the code: `grep -ic query README.md` returns **0** at this commit, while `routergroup.go` documents `MethodQuery` and `RouterGroup.Any` handling it. The README is where Go developers look for the routing surface.
2. `MethodQuery` is a hand-rolled stdlib shim, declared by hand because the standard library has no `http.MethodQuery` yet - two sources of truth for the same name once upstream ships it, and no tracked migration step in the tree.
3. Four exported entry points have no doc comment at all: `type ContextKeyType int` (`context.go:52`), `(*gin.Engine).Handler` (`gin.go:257`), `type SliceValidationError []error` (`binding/default_validator.go:21`) and `binding.MapFormWithTag` (`binding/form_mapping.go:40`). The last one is the costly omission - it is exported precisely so users can call the tag-aware form binder, and its tag semantics and pointer requirements are undiscoverable.
4. `(*gin.Context).BindWith` is deprecated but still exported and still in the reference (`deprecated.go:17`); it logs a deprecation warning on every call and there is no stated removal horizon in the tree.
5. The `ginS` package documents its 26 exported functions as wrappers for `Engine.X` but never says that the engine it wraps is a single process-global created with `sync.OnceValue` (`ginS/gins.go:16-18`) - the part a user needs before choosing it.

**Disclosure:** we are publishing this as part of a paid bounty that requires a credible public documentation site for a maintained third-party library, so there is a commercial reason for the page to exist. That is the only incentive involved; nothing here is sponsored by the gin project and we make no claim on it.

**The ask:** we are not asking you to take on a hosting burden. Any of these would be enough, in order of how much they help:

1. you host the generated reference on a `gin-gonic.com` page (or point us at the place you would want it),
2. you merge a small PR that adds the Sourcey build to this repository (so the reference is generated by the project itself, from `go.mod`, on every release),
3. you link to the reference from the README or the docs site,
4. or you tell us it is not worth having - then we will remove the page and report the result honestly.

The gaps listed above are the reason we think the reference is worth having for `gin` users: a generated API surface at a pinned commit, with the missing documentation and the undiscoverable `QUERY` support made explicit.

We are happy to open the PR ourselves. The build is two commands (`sourcey godoc -m . -p ./... -o godoc.json` and `sourcey build`) and the snapshot can be committed so the site is reproducible without a Go toolchain.

When a literal suffix follows a regexp placeholder, the placeholder's value can span a slash: `/re/{name:[^.]+}.json` serves `/re/a/b.json` with `name = "a/b"`, while the same regexp with nothing after it, and a plain `{name}.json`, both return 404 for a two-segment value:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"

	"github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
)

func main() {
	r := chi.NewRouter()
	echo := func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		fmt.Fprintf(w, "name=%q", chi.URLParam(r, "name"))
	}
	r.Get("/re/{name:[^.]+}.json", echo)
	r.Get("/bare/{name:[^.]+}", echo)
	r.Get("/plain/{name}.json", echo)
	for _, p := range []string{"/re/a.json", "/re/a/b.json", "/bare/a/b", "/plain/a/b.json"} {
		rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
		r.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", p, nil))
		fmt.Printf("GET %-16s -> %d %s\n", p, rec.Code, strings.TrimSpace(rec.Body.String()))
	}
}
```

Output:

```
GET /re/a.json       -> 200 name="a"
GET /re/a/b.json     -> 200 name="a/b"
GET /bare/a/b        -> 404 404 page not found
GET /plain/a/b.json  -> 404 404 page not found
```

The "URL patterns" documentation in chi.go says of a regexp placeholder that `/` will never be matched. I expected `GET /re/a/b.json` to be a 404 like the other two, rather than a match with a slash inside the parameter value.

Tested on chi v5.3.2 and on current master (3d1777a).

BTW, this was found by an automated program that writes property-based tests for various open source projects using [hegel](https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-go) (but it has been reviewed by hand before reporting). We've also potentially found (but not yet hand validated) 15 other bugs in chi. You can see the tests at https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-zoo/tree/main/targets/go/chi. Let us know if you would like us to file the other bugs found and/or contribute the tests. NB the tests are currently LLM generated and probably not yet suitable for inclusion as is, but we're happy to help get them into a better state if you want them.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"

	"github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
)

func main() {
	r := chi.NewRouter()
	echo := func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		fmt.Fprintf(w, "name=%q", chi.URLParam(r, "name"))
	}
	r.Get("/re/{name:[^.]+}.json", echo)
	r.Get("/bare/{name:[^.]+}", echo)
	r.Get("/plain/{name}.json", echo)
	for _, p := range []string{"/re/a.json", "/re/a/b.json", "/bare/a/b", "/plain/a/b.json"} {
		rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
		r.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", p, nil))
		fmt.Printf("GET %-16s -> %d %s\n", p, rec.Code, strings.TrimSpace(rec.Body.String()))
	}
}
```

Output:

```
GET /re/a.json       -> 200 name="a"
GET /re/a/b.json     -> 200 name="a/b"
GET /bare/a/b        -> 404 404 page not found
GET /plain/a/b.json  -> 404 404 page not found
```

The "URL patterns" documentation in chi.go says of a regexp placeholder that `/` will never be matched. I expected `GET /re/a/b.json` to be a 404 like the other two, rather than a match with a slash inside the parameter value.

Tested on chi v5.3.2 and on current master (3d1777a).

BTW, this was found by an automated program that writes property-based tests for various open source projects using [hegel](https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-go) (but it has been reviewed by hand before reporting). Let us know if you would like us to file the other bugs found and/or contribute the tests. ## Description

The contribution heatmap displays commits on the **push date** rather than the **commit author date**. This causes all commits pushed together to appear on the same day, even if they were authored on different days.

This is a continuation of #14051 and #11861 (both now locked).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create commits with backdated author timestamps:
   ```bash
   git commit --allow-empty --date="2025-01-20T15:00:00" -m "Commit from Jan 20"
   git commit --allow-empty --date="2025-01-22T19:30:00" -m "Commit from Jan 22"
   git commit --allow-empty --date="2025-01-24T14:15:00" -m "Commit from Jan 24"
   ```
2. Push all commits at once
3. Check the user's heatmap

## Expected Behavior

Commits should appear on their author dates (Jan 20, 22, 24) - matching GitHub's behavior.

## Actual Behavior

All commits appear on the push date (e.g., Jan 27).

## Solution

PR #36469 fixes this by:
- Adding an `original_unix` field to the Action model to store the commit author timestamp
- Grouping commits by date and creating separate action records for each date
- Updating the heatmap query to use `COALESCE(NULLIF(original_unix, 0), created_unix)`

The fix maintains backward compatibility - existing records continue using the push date.

## Version

Tested on latest main branch (commit from January 2026)

body_text: ### Description This issue consolidates some UI/UX issues in #18546 and 16285, and proposes a UI implementation of the request. To summarize: * "Initialize" is an improper name to apply to the _.gitignore_, _License_, and _README_ files as it creates confusion with `git init` (e.g. https://git-scm.com/docs/git-init). (It is recommended to instead refer to these as _Bootstrap Files_, and will be referred to as such in the remainder of this issue to avoid ambiguity with the actual initialization of a repository.) * There is no way to suppress creation of *individual* bootstrap files (e.g. one cannot choose to bootstrap with a .gitignore but NOT a README, etc.) * There is no support for alternate/non-Markdown README files, even if renderers are set up for them ( #18546 ) * There is no support for specifying the target filename for the README ( #16285 ) * There is no support for specifying the target filename for the LICENSE * The bootstrap files are not properly visually separated from the remainder of repo creation options ### Screenshots ## Current Implementation ## Proposed Implementation **No bootstrap files enabled** **All bootstrap files enabled, with multiple .gitignore entries** **Only .gitignore is enabled** ### NOTE The .gitignore selection will probably need its JS tweaked a fair bit; I have it reimplemented here just as a simple multi-select HTML box for simplicity. I was also trying to bang out something quick so I didn't include the text input fields for the README/LICENSE filenames but presumably that could be easy enough to add. ### Gitea Version 1.25.4 ### Can you reproduce the bug on the Gitea demo site? Yes ### Operating System ArchLinux ### Browser Version Brave 1.87.191 (Official Build) (64-bit) (Based off of Chromium: 145.0.7632.120)

body_text:
### Feature Description

Since we have support for branch level push and pull ACL, can this feature be used to implement the ability to push local-only branches on mirrored repos? 

I understand that currently Gitea doesnt support pushing to mirrors because it would have to automate conflict resolution, and if I were to push my local branch upstream it would also result in conflicts. But I would be willing to compromise with Gitea nuking my local branch and making it read-only if I did.

I propose mirrors can use the ACL as a whitelist, where you can specify which branches allow push vs regular repos where you can push by default.

The current translations are using go-specific printf-style placeholders, for example a hyptothetical `%[1]s committed %[2]s on %[3]s`. Such strings are very hard to translate correctly without context because the user does not know what those placeholders represent.

We should replace with format `{user} committed {hash} on {date}` which has multiple benefits:

1. Translator immediately has full context
2. Translator can easily re-order placeholders how they see fit

https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/37119#issuecomment-4240284707 is related

I think most people are building gitea with `bindata` to generate a self-contained binary, so I would suggest adding `bindata` do the default tags and introduce a `nobindata` tag for bindata-less builds.

This will be a breaking change only for people who built without bindata, which I think is a miniscule amount.

body_text:
### Summary

The swagger annotations on `routers/api/v1/**` endpoints only document HTTP responses returned directly by the handler. Responses produced by the middleware layer (auth, scope checks, permission checks) — notably `401 Unauthorized` and `403 Forbidden` — are **not** documented on most endpoints, but the few endpoints whose handlers happen to also return 403 directly do document it. This produces an inconsistent and misleading OpenAPI spec.

### Example

In `routers/api/v1/user/gpg_key.go`, all endpoints are protected by the same auth/scope middleware, yet:

- `ListGPGKeys`, `ListMyGPGKeys`, `GetGPGKey`, `CreateGPGKey` — document only `200`/`201`/`404`/`422`, no `403`.
- `DeleteUserPublicKey` (`routers/api/v1/user/key.go`) — documents `403` because the handler itself calls `ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, ...)`.

A client generated from the spec has no way to know that every authenticated endpoint can respond with `401`/`403` from the middleware.

### Background

Noticed during review of #37271 — removing a never-reached `IsErrGPGKeyAccessDenied` branch caused `DeleteGPGKey`'s handler to no longer return `403`, prompting a review comment asking whether the swagger `403` was still valid. The answer turned out to be ''per existing convention, no'', because the convention only covers handler-direct responses — but the convention itself is arguably wrong/incomplete.

### Proposal

Pick one policy and apply it consistently:

1. **Explicit everywhere:** add `401` / `403` / (maybe `500`) to every authenticated/scoped endpoint's swagger annotation. Verbose but honest.
2. **Implicit via global responses:** declare these middleware responses once at the swagger/OpenAPI top level (security scheme default responses) and drop per-endpoint duplication entirely.
3. **Templated helper:** introduce a swagger-comment shorthand / code generator so endpoint authors can't forget.

Option 2 is likely the cleanest if the tooling supports it.

This issue is not blocking anything; filing it so the refactor isn't forgotten.

---
This issue was written with the help of Claude Opus 4.7

{"repository": "go-gitea/gitea", "task_candidate_id": 5149, "repository_id": 105, "issue_number": 37307, "github_issue_id": 4293501259, "html_url": "https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues/37307", "created_at": "2026-04-20T06:14:28+00:00", "author_association": "MEMBER", "title": "Inconsistent swagger documentation of middleware-origin responses (401/403)", "body_text": "### Summary

The swagger annotations on `routers/api/v1/**` endpoints only document HTTP responses returned directly by the handler. Responses produced by the middleware layer (auth, scope checks, permission checks) — notably `401 Unauthorized` and `403 Forbidden` — are **not** documented on most endpoints, but the few endpoints whose handlers happen to also return 403 directly do document it. This produces an inconsistent and misleading OpenAPI spec.

### Example

In `routers/api/v1/user/gpg_key.go`, all endpoints are protected by the same auth/scope middleware, yet:

- `ListGPGKeys`, `ListMyGPGKeys`, `GetGPGKey`, `CreateGPGKey` — document only `200`/`201`/`404`/`422`, no `403`.
- `DeleteUserPublicKey` (`routers/api/v1/user/key.go`) — documents `403` because the handler itself calls `ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, ...)`.

A client generated from the spec has no way to know that every authenticated endpoint can respond with `401`/`403` from the middleware.

### Background

Noticed during review of #37271 — removing a never-reached `IsErrGPGKeyAccessDenied` branch caused `DeleteGPGKey`'s handler to no longer return `403`, prompting a review comment asking whether the swagger `403` was still valid. The answer turned out to be ''per existing convention, no'', because the convention only covers handler-direct responses — but the convention itself is arguably wrong/incomplete.

### Proposal

Pick one policy and apply it consistently:

1. **Explicit everywhere:** add `401` / `403` / (maybe `500`) to every authenticated/scoped endpoint's swagger annotation. Verbose but honest.
2. **Implicit via global responses:** declare these middleware responses once at the swagger/OpenAPI top level (security scheme default responses) and drop per-endpoint duplication entirely.
3. **Templated helper:** introduce a swagger-comment shorthand / code generator so endpoint authors can't forget.

Option 2 is likely the cleanest if the tooling supports it.

This issue is not blocking anything; filing it so the refactor isn't forgotten.

## Description

Pushing images to the Gitea container registry with `docker buildx build --push`
intermittently fails a layer-upload initiation with:

```
unexpected status from POST request to https://<registry>/v2/<owner>/<image>/blobs/uploads/: 401 Unauthorized: reqPackageAccess
```

The failure is **intermittent and per-push**: in a CI matrix that pushes ~12
images, a rotating ~1–3 of them fail this way on any given run, while the rest
succeed with the *same* credential. A plain re-run usually succeeds.

It is **not** an auth/scope misconfiguration: the same access token authenticates
successfully on other requests in the very same push (the `GET /v2/token` returns
200 and `HEAD .../blobs/<digest>` on the same connection returns 200/404), and
the package is correctly linked to its repository.

## Environment

- Gitea **1.26.2**, PostgreSQL database.
- Container registry, push via BuildKit (`docker buildx build --push`) from a CI
  runner; several images pushed concurrently, and BuildKit issues many parallel
  requests per push (speculative blob-existence `HEAD` probes + upload inits) and
  **cancels** the redundant ones.
- Reproducible only with BuildKit, **not** with `curl` (even 20 concurrent `curl`
  POSTs to `/blobs/uploads/` all return 202) — because `curl` reads every response
  and never cancels an in-flight request.

## Root cause analysis

The `ContainerRoutes` middleware chain runs, in order:

```
verifyAuth → UserAssignmentWeb → PackageAssignment → reqPackageAccess
```

When BuildKit cancels an in-flight request (which it does aggressively during a
push), the request's `context` is cancelled. That cancellation aborts the
in-flight database query in `UserAssignmentWeb` / `PackageAssignment`:

```
services/context/user.go:25 ... UserAssignmentWeb: GetUserByName: context canceled
services/context/user.go:25 ... UserAssignmentWeb: GetUserByName: pq: canceling statement due to user request (57014)
```

Depending on exactly where the cancellation lands in the chain, two outcomes are
observed for sibling requests of the same push:

1. **500** — when `GetUserByName` returns the cancellation as an error
   (`UserAssignmentWeb` → 500, `HeadBlob` → 500 "context canceled").
2. **401** — when the cancelled/cut-short load leaves `ctx.Package.AccessMode` at
   its zero value (`AccessModeNone`). `reqPackageAccess`
   (`routers/api/packages/api.go`) then hits its second gate:

   ```go
   if ctx.Package.AccessMode < accessMode && !ctx.IsUserSiteAdmin() {
       ... HTTPError(http.StatusUnauthorized, "reqPackageAccess", ...)
   }
   ```

   and returns **401** in well under 1 ms (a pure in-memory comparison —
   confirming the access mode was never populated, rather than a real permission
   denial). The bearer token's scope check (the first gate) passes; it is
   specifically the package access-mode that is empty.

So the 401 and the 500s are the **same underlying event** — a cancelled
auth-context DB query — surfacing at different points in the middleware chain.

### Representative log excerpt (single push, single instant)

```
GET  /v2/token?...scope=repository:<owner>/<image>:pull,push  → 200 OK   (container.Authenticate)
HEAD /v2/<owner>/<image>/blobs/<sha256:...>                    → 200 OK   (container.HeadBlob)
HEAD /v2/<owner>/<image>/blobs/<sha256:...>                    → 404      (container.HeadBlob)
POST /v2/<owner>/<image>/blobs/uploads/                        → 401 Unauthorized in 0.6ms (packages.reqPackageAccess)
[E] HeadBlob: 500 context canceled                              (container.go:523)
[E] UserAssignmentWeb: GetUserByName: context canceled          (services/context/user.go:25)
[E] UserAssignmentWeb: GetUserByName: pq: canceling statement due to user request (57014)
```

## Expected behaviour

A cancelled client request must not degrade to a **401**. Either:

- propagate the cancellation as a clear client-cancelled status (e.g. 499 /
  context-canceled 5xx) so the client can retry cleanly, **or**
- ensure `reqPackageAccess` distinguishes "access mode not loaded due to a
  failed/cancelled assignment" from "access genuinely denied" (e.g. fail closed
  with a 5xx when `PackageAssignment`/`UserAssignmentWeb` did not complete,
  rather than emitting a 401 from a zero-value `AccessMode`).

A spurious 401 is especially harmful for container pushes because clients treat
401 as an auth failure (abort), not a transient/retryable condition.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Gitea 1.26.2 with the container registry enabled (PostgreSQL backend).
2. Build N images and push them concurrently with `docker buildx build --push`
   (BuildKit's parallel blob probing + cancellation is the trigger). A CI matrix
   pushing ~12 images reproduces ~1–3 failures per run.
3. Observe intermittent `401 Unauthorized: reqPackageAccess` on
   `POST /blobs/uploads/`, alongside `GetUserByName: context canceled` / `57014`
   errors in the Gitea log at the same instant.

Note: not reproducible with sequential or non-cancelling clients (`docker push`
classic, `curl`).

## Additional notes

- Tested across Gitea 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 — same behaviour; `reqPackageAccess`
  itself is byte-identical between the two.
- Serializing the pushes across CI jobs with an external mutex does **not** help —
  a push fails even when it is the only one pushing, because the cancellation is
  *intra-push* (one buildx push cancels its own sibling requests).

### Gitea Version

1.26.4

### What happened?

Hi,
I want to create a new repository for my organization. After clicking create repository I will get the following error
~~~
500 Internal Server Error
Ein Fehler ist aufgetreten:

CreatePost, initRepository: SyncRepoBranches: Error 1364 (HY000): Field 'id' doesn't have a default value
Gitea-Version: 1.26.4

Wenn du glaubst, dass dies ein Fehler von Gitea ist, suche bitte auf [GitHub](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues) nach diesem Fehler und erstelle gegebenenfalls einen neuen Bugreport.
~~~

I run gitea at a docker container on my Synology NAS and with a MariaDB connection to a MariaDB 10.11.11 server.

Do you have a tip for the solution?

Thank you for your help
BR
Martin

### How are you running Gitea?

Docker Container on Synology NAS.

body_text:
## Description

Running Gitea as a multi-replica Kubernetes `Deployment` against a single shared NFS-backed RWX volume produces intermittent HTTP 500s on the contents API, even when every documented HA prerequisite is satisfied. The failure is a read-after-write visibility gap between replicas, and I don't think it is fixable by application-level locking — which seems worth recording as its own issue rather than only as a note on the broader clustering discussion in #13791.

Two distinct problems are described below. The second one is a straightforward improvement that is worth applying at any replica count.

## Gitea Version

1.25.x

## How are you running Gitea?

Official Helm chart, Kubernetes `Deployment` with `replicaCount: 2`:

- One shared RWX volume (AWS EFS, NFSv4.1) holding `/data`, mounted at the same path on both pods
- External PostgreSQL
- Redis-compatible instance wired for cache, session and queues
- `ISSUE_INDEXER_TYPE: db`, `REPO_INDEXER_ENABLED: false`

This satisfies every prerequisite in the HA documentation and in the chart's `docs/ha-setup.md`. Single-replica deployments with an otherwise identical configuration have never reproduced it.

## Description of the bug

The workload is programmatic: repeated `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents` writing small files to a branch. Every few hundred calls returns HTTP 500 with:

```
SetDefaultIndex: exit status 128 - fatal: unable to read tree (<sha>)
```

and sometimes, one level up:

```
object does not exist [id: refs/heads/<branch>, rel_path: ]
```

The object named in the error was written seconds earlier by a request that **succeeded**, served by the *other* replica. Nothing is corrupt — `git fsck` is clean, and reading the same object later always succeeds.

## Root cause

This is not a storage consistency problem. EFS is strongly consistent server-side. The staleness is in the Linux NFS client on each node, which caches attributes and directory entries (`acdirmin`/`acdirmax` default to 30s/60s) and, with the default `lookupcache=all`, caches **negative** lookups as well.

Git addresses objects by literal path (`objects/de/e7f8…`) and refs by literal file. When replica A creates a new loose object and ref, replica B's kernel can serve a cached negative dentry for that exact path for up to the cache window, so git correctly reports the object as missing.

The contents API is especially exposed because of the temp-repo pattern in `services/repository/files/temp_repo.go`:

```go
// Clone — services/repository/files/temp_repo.go:57
cmd := gitcmd.NewCommand("clone", "-s", "-b").AddDynamicArguments(branch, t.repo.RepoPath(), t.basePath)

// SetDefaultIndex — services/repository/files/temp_repo.go:101
if _, _, err := gitcmd.NewCommand("read-tree", "HEAD").RunStdString(ctx, &gitcmd.RunOpts{Dir: t.basePath}); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("SetDefaultIndex: %w", err)
}
```

`clone -s` means objects are never copied — `objects/info/alternates` points straight back at the shared object store — so `read-tree` resolves the tree through the shared volume using the *serving* replica's NFS client cache. A read on replica B of an object just written by replica A is precisely the unsafe operation.

### Why a distributed lock does not fix this

I checked where `globallock` is actually used on `release/v1.25`:

- `routers/api/packages/{maven,container}`, `services/packages/arch`
- `modules/gitrepo/{config,remote}.go`
- `services/versioned_migration`
- `services/repository/transfer.go`
- `services/pull/{pull,check,update,merge}.go`
- `services/wiki/wiki.go`
- `services/mirror/mirror_pull.go`

Nothing under `services/repository/files/`. So the contents API write path — arguably the most common programmatic write into a repository — currently has no cross-replica mutual exclusion at all.

But adding one there would **not** fix this failure. A lock serializes writers; it cannot invalidate the *reader's* NFS attribute/dentry cache. Replica B can acquire the lock cleanly, with replica A's write fully committed and the lock released, and still not see the object. Read-after-write coherence across nodes is a property of the filesystem mount, not something the application can supply.

That distinction seems important, because "add a global lock" is the natural reading of the remaining clustering work in #13791, and for shared-filesystem git storage it is necessary but not sufficient.

## Second issue: temp clones land on the shared volume by default

`CreateTemporaryPath` resolves to `AppDataTempDir()`, which falls back to `${APP_DATA_PATH}/tmp` when `[server] APP_TEMP_PATH` is unset (`modules/setting/path.go`):

```go
func AppDataTempDir(sub string) *tempdir.TempDir {
	if appTempPathInternal != "" {
		return tempdir.New(appTempPathInternal, "gitea-tmp/"+sub)
	}
	return tempdir.New(AppDataPath, "tmp/"+sub)
}
```

On a shared-volume install that puts **every** temp clone on the network filesystem. Confirmed empirically — three `POST /contents` calls against a stock 1.25.x produced three temp clones under the data path:

```
APP_DATA_PATH = /data/gitea
  APP_TEMP_PATH: (not set)
/data/gitea/tmp/local-repo/upload.git1127329404
/data/gitea/tmp/local-repo/upload.git126396543
/data/gitea/tmp/local-repo/upload.git2313201698
```

Pointing `APP_TEMP_PATH` at node-local scratch made our writes measurably faster and is safe at any replica count. Note also that these directories leak on an unclean shutdown, so on a shared volume they accumulate permanently.

Would it make sense to document this as recommended for shared-volume deployments, or to have the Helm chart default it to the pod-local `emptyDir` it already mounts?

## Expected behaviour

Either multi-replica deployments on a shared RWX volume serve reads coherently, or the documented HA prerequisites state the cache-coherence property the volume must provide.

The current prerequisite reads:

> Shared git repository storage: a POSIX volume (NFS/Gluster/NetApp) mounted at the same path on every node

A default-mounted NFS volume is not POSIX-equivalent for git's read-after-write on newly created files, so following the prerequisites exactly still yields intermittent 500s. Documenting the required mount options would save operators from discovering this in production.

## Workarounds, for anyone hitting this

1. **Mount options on the git volume** — `lookupcache=none,actimeo=0` (or `noac`) forces every lookup to the server, which is correct given EFS's server-side consistency. It works, but git stats thousands of files per operation, so the latency cost is significant. Scoping it to the repositories path only, and keeping temp clones local via `APP_TEMP_PATH`, makes it more tolerable.
2. **Repository-affinity routing** — consistent-hash on the `{owner}/{repo}` path segment in front of the replicas so a given repository is only ever served by one node. Removes cross-node read-after-write in steady state; the window returns only while the hash ring shifts during a restart.
3. **One writer** — what we did as an immediate mitigation, at the cost of the availability the extra replica was there to provide. This also requires `maxSurge: 0` on the Deployment, since the chart's default rolling update briefly runs two pods against the same volume and reintroduces the bug on every deploy.

## Related

- #13791 — the Gitea Cluster proposal. This issue is the concrete read-after-write case, plus the finding that `globallock` does not cover the failing path and could not fix it if it did.
- The chart's `docs/ha-setup.md` known limitation that cron runs on all replicas is relevant here too: `repo_health_check` (`git fsck`) runs on every node against the same shared repositories, and `check_repo_stats` runs at every startup on every node. `git_gc_repos` is disabled by default, which is fortunate — concurrent `git gc --prune` from multiple nodes against one shared object store would be a corruption risk rather than a 500.

Happy to provide more detail or test patches on a multi-replica NFS setup.

{"repository": "go-gitea/gitea", "task_candidate_id": 5157, "repository_id": 105, "issue_number": 39282, "github_issue_id": 5396478503, "html_url": "https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues/39282", "created_at": "2026-09-09T07:36:56+00:00", "author_association": "CONTRIBUTOR", "title": "HA on shared NFS/EFS: contents API returns 500 due to cross-replica read-after-write staleness, and globallock does not cover the path", "body_text": "## Description

Running Gitea as a multi-replica Kubernetes `Deployment` against a single shared NFS-backed RWX volume produces intermittent HTTP 500s on the contents API, even when every documented HA prerequisite is satisfied. The failure is a read-after-write visibility gap between replicas, and I don't think it is fixable by application-level locking — which seems worth recording as its own issue rather than only as a note on the broader clustering discussion in #13791.

Two distinct problems are described below. The second one is a straightforward improvement that is worth applying at any replica count.

## Gitea Version

1.25.x

## How are you running Gitea?

Official Helm chart, Kubernetes `Deployment` with `replicaCount: 2`:

- One shared RWX volume (AWS EFS, NFSv4.1) holding `/data`, mounted at the same path on both pods
- External PostgreSQL
- Redis-compatible instance wired for cache, session and queues
- `ISSUE_INDEXER_TYPE: db`, `REPO_INDEXER_ENABLED: false`

This satisfies every prerequisite in the HA documentation and in the chart's `docs/ha-setup.md`. Single-replica deployments with an otherwise identical configuration have never reproduced it.

## Description of the bug

The workload is programmatic: repeated `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents` writing small files to a branch. Every few hundred calls returns HTTP 500 with:

```
SetDefaultIndex: exit status 128 - fatal: unable to read tree (<sha>)
```

and sometimes, one level up:

```
object does not exist [id: refs/heads/<branch>, rel_path: ]
```

The object named in the error was written seconds earlier by a request that **succeeded**, served by the *other* replica. Nothing is corrupt — `git fsck` is clean, and reading the same object later always succeeds.

## Root cause

This is not a storage consistency problem. EFS is strongly consistent server-side. The staleness is in the Linux NFS client on each node, which caches attributes and directory entries (`acdirmin`/`acdirmax` default to 30s/60s) and, with the default `lookupcache=all`, caches **negative** lookups as well.

Git addresses objects by literal path (`objects/de/e7f8…`) and refs by literal file. When replica A creates a new loose object and ref, replica B's kernel can serve a cached negative dentry for that exact path for up to the cache window, so git correctly reports the object as missing.

The contents API is especially exposed because of the temp-repo pattern in `services/repository/files/temp_repo.go`:

```go
// Clone — services/repository/files/temp_repo.go:57
cmd := gitcmd.NewCommand("clone", "-s", "-b").AddDynamicArguments(branch, t.repo.RepoPath(), t.basePath)

// SetDefaultIndex — services/repository/files/temp_repo.go:101
if _, _, err := gitcmd.NewCommand("read-tree", "HEAD").RunStdString(ctx, &gitcmd.RunOpts{Dir: t.basePath}); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("SetDefaultIndex: %w", err)
}
```

`clone -s` means objects are never copied — `objects/info/alternates` points straight back at the shared object store — so `read-tree` resolves the tree through the shared volume using the *serving* replica's NFS client cache. A read on replica B of an object just written by replica A is precisely the unsafe operation.

### Why a distributed lock does not fix this

I checked where `globallock` is actually used on `release/v1.25`:

- `routers/api/packages/{maven,container}`, `services/packages/arch`
- `modules/gitrepo/{config,remote}.go`
- `services/versioned_migration`
- `services/repository/transfer.go`
- `services/pull/{pull,check,update,merge}.go`
- `services/wiki/wiki.go`
- `services/mirror/mirror_pull.go`

Nothing under `services/repository/files/`. So the contents API write path — arguably the most common programmatic write into a repository — currently has no cross-replica mutual exclusion at all.

But adding one there would **not** fix this failure. A lock serializes writers; it cannot invalidate the *reader's* NFS attribute/dentry cache. Replica B can acquire the lock cleanly, with replica A's write fully committed and the lock released, and still not see the object. Read-after-write coherence across nodes is a property of the filesystem mount, not something the application can supply.

That distinction seems important, because "add a global lock" is the natural reading of the remaining clustering work in #13791, and for shared-filesystem git storage it is necessary but not sufficient.

## Second issue: temp clones land on the shared volume by default

`CreateTemporaryPath` resolves to `AppDataTempDir()`, which falls back to `${APP_DATA_PATH}/tmp` when `[server] APP_TEMP_PATH` is unset (`modules/setting/path.go`):

```go
func AppDataTempDir(sub string) *tempdir.TempDir {
	if appTempPathInternal != "" {
		return tempdir.New(appTempPathInternal, "gitea-tmp/"+sub)
	}
	return tempdir.New(AppDataPath, "tmp/"+sub)
}
```

On a shared-volume install that puts **every** temp clone on the network filesystem. Confirmed empirically — three `POST /contents` calls against a stock 1.25.x produced three temp clones under the data path:

```
APP_DATA_PATH = /data/gitea
  APP_TEMP_PATH: (not set)
/data/gitea/tmp/local-repo/upload.git1127329404
/data/gitea/tmp/local-repo/upload.git126396543
/data/gitea/tmp/local-repo/upload.git2313201698
```

Pointing `APP_TEMP_PATH` at node-local scratch made our writes measurably faster and is safe at any replica count. Note also that these directories leak on an unclean shutdown, so on a shared volume they accumulate permanently.

Would it make sense to document this as recommended for shared-volume deployments, or to have the Helm chart default it to the pod-local `emptyDir` it already mounts?

## Expected behaviour

Either multi-replica deployments on a shared RWX volume serve reads coherently, or the documented HA prerequisites state the cache-coherence property the volume must provide.

The current prerequisite reads:

> Shared git repository storage: a POSIX volume (NFS/Gluster/NetApp) mounted at the same path on every node

A default-mounted NFS volume is not POSIX-equivalent for git's read-after-write on newly created files, so following the prerequisites exactly still yields intermittent 500s. Documenting the required mount options would save operators from discovering this in production.

## Workarounds, for anyone hitting this

1. **Mount options on the git volume** — `lookupcache=none,actimeo=0` (or `noac`) forces every lookup to the server, which is correct given EFS's server-side consistency. It works, but git stats thousands of files per operation, so the latency cost is significant. Scoping it to the repositories path only, and keeping temp clones local via `APP_TEMP_PATH`, makes it more tolerable.
2. **Repository-affinity routing** — consistent-hash on the `{owner}/{repo}` path segment in front of the replicas so a given repository is only ever served by one node. Removes cross-node read-after-write in steady state; the window returns only while the hash ring shifts during a restart.
3. **One writer** — what we did as an immediate mitigation, at the cost of the availability the extra replica was there to provide. This also requires `maxSurge: 0` on the Deployment, since the chart's default rolling update briefly runs two pods against the same volume and reintroduces the bug on every deploy.

## Related

- #13791 — the Gitea Cluster proposal. This issue is the concrete read-after-write case, plus the finding that `globallock` does not cover the failing path and could not fix it if it did.
- The chart's `docs/ha-setup.md` known limitation that cron runs on all replicas is relevant here too: `repo_health_check` (`git fsck`) runs on every node against the same shared repositories, and `check_repo_stats` runs at every startup on every node. `git_gc_repos` is disabled by default, which is fortunate — concurrent `git gc --prune` from multiple nodes against one shared object store would be a corruption risk rather than a 500.

Happy to provide more detail or test patches on a multi-replica NFS setup.

## Description

`git clone` / full `git fetch` over both HTTPS and SSH consistently fails with:

```
fatal: early EOF
fatal: fetch-pack: invalid index-pack output
```

or on the client side sometimes:

```
fatal: protocol error: bad pack header
```

This reproduces 100% of the time for a full clone (or even a single-branch clone with no local `have`s) of one specific repository, on a self-hosted instance, while small incremental fetches against the same repo succeed normally. It reproduces identically on Gitea 1.24.5 and 1.27.3 (upgraded mid-investigation), across git clients 2.53.0 and 2.54.0 (Windows), over protocol v0 and v2, and over both HTTP and SSH transports.

## Environment

- Gitea 1.24.5 and 1.27.3 (both tested, same result) — official `docker.gitea.com/gitea` Docker image
- DB: MySQL/MariaDB
- Reverse proxy: nginx 1.18.0 (confirmed **not** the cause, see below)
- Repo: ~2.1 GB single pack (already gc'd with a bitmap index), ~50 branches + PR refs, includes Git LFS content (LFS not involved in the failing transfer itself)
- Git client: git for Windows 2.53.0.windows.1 and 2.54.0.windows.1
- Auth tested: Basic auth with a Personal Access Token, and GCM's automatic OAuth2 flow (`Server auth using Basic with user 'OAUTH_USER'`) — both fail identically

## What I ruled out

- **Repo/pack corruption**: `git fsck --full` clean, `git verify-pack` OK.
- **A local (non-network) clone of the same bare repo, using the git binary directly, succeeds fully** (full checkout of ~17k files, ~40s).
- **Manually replaying the exact captured negotiation bytes directly into `git upload-pack --stateless-rpc <repo>` (same container, same user, same cwd) produces a full, valid ~2.2 GB pack.** See below — this is the same exact bytes Gitea itself fed to `git upload-pack` in the failing live request.
- **nginx**: bypassed entirely (tested directly against the container's internal IP:3000, and against `127.0.0.1:<mapped-port>`), same failure. Confirmed `proxy_buffering off`, HTTP/1.1 forced (no h2), `client_max_body_size 0`, generous timeouts already in place (there's a known history of nginx+HTTP/2 corrupting large packs on this same install, already fixed by disabling h2; this is a separate issue).
- **docker-proxy / port publishing**: bypassed, tested directly against the container network IP.
- **Memory/OOM**: container limit raised to 10g (host has 11GB + swap); `docker stats` before/after shows no memory pressure; `pack.threads=1` + `pack.windowMemory=512M` in `[git.config]` made no difference. (There are other open Gitea issues, e.g. #35996, #31036, describing OOM-killed `pack-objects` with this exact client-facing symptom — that is **not** what's happening here, see below.)
- **Client git version**: 2.53.0 and 2.54.0 both fail identically.
- **Protocol version**: `protocol.version=0` and `=2` both fail identically.
- **Request size / branch count**: fails even for `--single-branch` clone of just one ref (smallest possible negotiation).
- **Connection reuse**: forcing `Connection: close` (fresh TCP+TLS per request) makes no difference.
- **Transport**: SSH fails identically to HTTPS (after fixing an unrelated local misconfiguration where the container's `SSH_PORT`/`SSH_LISTEN_PORT` env vars weren't set to match the externally published port — worth calling out since it's an easy footgun: the built-in OpenSSH service only reads `SSH_PORT`/`SSH_LISTEN_PORT` env vars, independent of `app.ini`'s `[server] SSH_PORT`).

## The key evidence

I wrapped `/usr/bin/git` inside the container with a shim that logs argv + exit code, and (for the actual RPC call, not `--advertise-refs`) captures stdin/stdout to files:

```
[WRAP] ... ARGS: upload-pack --stateless-rpc --advertise-refs .
[WRAP] ... EXIT: 0 (advertise-refs, no stdin capture)
[WRAP] ... ARGS: upload-pack --stateless-rpc .
[WRAP] ... EXIT: 0 STDIN_BYTES: 2383 STDOUT_BYTES: 12
```

- `STDIN_BYTES: 2383` — captured to a file, inspected byte-for-byte: a fully well-formed, complete pkt-line `want ... done` negotiation (single branch, in this instance). Gzip decompression (`Content-Encoding: gzip` from the client, handled in `serviceRPC()`) is clearly working correctly — the decompressed bytes are correct and complete.
- `STDOUT_BYTES: 12` — i.e. just `NAK` + flush, no pack at all, and the outer `git.Run()` / HTTP request completed with `200 OK` (or, in the SSH case, the session just ends) as if nothing went wrong.
- **Replaying those exact 2383 captured bytes** (`git upload-pack --stateless-rpc . < captured-stdin.bin`, same container, same cwd, same repo) **produces a full ~2.2 GB valid pack.**

So: identical binary, identical repository, identical negotiation input (byte-for-byte, verified), identical container/user/cwd — but the live invocation via Gitea's own `serviceRPC` (`WithStdinCopy` from the decompressed request body / `WithStdoutCopy` to `ctx.Resp` over HTTP, or the equivalent SSH command path) produces essentially nothing, while a manual replay of the exact same bytes produces a complete pack.

On one occasion the live command's exit code was `141` (SIGPIPE) instead of `0`, and this **was** logged normally:

```
routers/web/repo/githttp.go:421:serviceRPC() [E] Fail to serve RPC(upload-pack) in <owner>/<repo>.git: exit status 141 -
```

with empty stderr. Most of the time it's a silent, non-error exit 0, which — if it's going through `IsErrorCanceledOrKilled` logic somewhere for the SSH path, or some other cancellation, or whether it's just "genuinely no error" — isn't visible in logs at any log level up to `trace`.

## Question / ask

Given the manual-replay-of-exact-same-bytes test, this looks less like a decompression bug and more like something in how the actual command invocation's stdout pipe is being consumed/closed early specifically for this repo/negotiation combination (maybe something size- or timing-dependent that a purely local, unhurried manual replay doesn't trigger). I don't have a Go debugger attached to reproduce further; happy to run any additional diagnostics (I have full root access to the box and can reproduce on demand).

Is there a known class of bug here, or a next diagnostic step (e.g., a way to get more detail out of the process manager / context cancellation path) that would help narrow this down further?

### Gitea Version

1.27.3

### What happened?

## Summary

When a Gitea Actions workflow attempts to use a **public composite action** hosted on the same Gitea instance under a different user or organization (e.g. `uses: https://git.example.com/shared-org/my-action.git@v1`), the runner (`act_runner`) fails during the action download phase with:

```text
Unable to clone https://git.example.com/shared-org/my-action.git refs/heads/v1: repository not found: Repository not found
Error: repository not found: Repository not found
```

> **Note:** This behavior was tested on a single Gitea instance (across different users/organizations). I have **not** tested accessing actions **from one Gitea instance to another**.

### The Authentication Paradox
* The repository `shared-org/my-action` is **100% public**.
* An anonymous user or container running `git clone https://git.example.com/shared-org/my-action.git` succeeds without credentials (`HTTP 200`).
* However, when executed inside a workflow via `uses:`, `act_runner` automatically attaches the calling job's `GITEA_TOKEN` to the Git clone request.
* Because the job is running in a different repository (e.g. `calling-org/my-app`) and `DEFAULT_ACTIONS_TOKEN_PERMISSION = restricted` is configured, Gitea restricts the token strictly to the calling repository.
* When Gitea's Smart HTTP handler evaluates the request with the attached token, it detects that the token does not have scope for `shared-org/my-action`, and responds with **`404 Not Found`** (to avoid leaking private repo existence).
* `act_runner` (`go-git`) maps that `404` directly to `repository not found: Repository not found`.

**Result:** Presenting a valid Gitea Actions token gives **less access** to a public repository than presenting no credentials at all.

---

## This Affects Two Key Scenarios

1. **Scenario A — Public Instance with `DEFAULT_ACTIONS_TOKEN_PERMISSION = restricted`:**
   * `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = false`
   * The action repo is public, but cross-owner actions cannot be consumed via standard `uses:` because the restricted token is rejected with `404`.
2. **Scenario B — Private Instance with `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = true` (re: #28187):**
   * Even when an internal action repository is meant to be shared across the entire instance, workflows in different organizations cannot clone it because the automatic job token is scoped only to its own repository/organization.

---

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Gitea with `DEFAULT_ACTIONS_TOKEN_PERMISSION = restricted` in `app.ini` / environment:
   ```ini
   [actions]
   DEFAULT_ACTIONS_TOKEN_PERMISSION = restricted
   ```
2. Create a **public** repository containing a composite action under User A (e.g. `user-a/hello-action`).
3. In a repository under Org B (e.g. `org-b/my-app`), create a workflow referencing User A's action:
   ```yaml
   name: Test Action
   on: [push]
   jobs:
     test:
       runs-on: ubuntu-latest
       steps:
         - uses: https://git.example.com/user-a/hello-action.git@main
   ```
4. Trigger the workflow.
5. `act_runner` will fail to download the action, reporting `repository not found: Repository not found`.

---

## Technical Analysis & Root Cause

1. **In `act_runner` (`pkg/runner/step_action_remote.go`):**
   When `act_runner` prepares to download a remote action, it unconditionally injects the job token:
   ```go
   gitClone := stepActionRemoteNewCloneExecutor(git.NewGitCloneExecutorInput{
       URL:   sar.remoteAction.CloneURL(),
       Token: github.Token, // Automatically injects GITEA_TOKEN
   })
   ```
   There is no workflow syntax option in `uses:` to specify an anonymous clone.

2. **In Gitea HTTP Git Backend (`routers/web/repo/githttp.go` & `services/context/permission.go`):**
   When `GET /<owner>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack` arrives:
   * If unauthenticated, `canAnonymousPull` evaluates to `true` for public repositories, and access is granted (`200 OK`).
   * If authenticated (`ctx.IsSigned == true`), Gitea invokes `context.CheckRepoScopedToken(ctx, repo, ...)` to enforce token scopes.
   * Under `restricted` mode, the Actions token only has permissions for the calling repo, failing `CheckRepoScopedToken`.
   * Gitea returns `404 Not Found`, breaking `go-git`'s clone.

---

## Working Workaround

Instead of letting `act_runner` attempt to clone the remote action with its injected `GITEA_TOKEN`, fetch the action repository into a local subfolder in a preceding step, then reference it as a local composite action (`uses: ./<path>`):

```yaml
    - name: Fetch Shared Action
      run: |
        rm -rf .gitea/actions/shared-action
        # For public instances (Scenario A): anonymous git clone works without credentials
        git clone --depth 1 --branch v1 https://git.example.com/user-a/shared-action.git .gitea/actions/shared-action

        # For private instances (Scenario B): authenticate via deploy key or secret PAT
        # git clone --depth 1 --branch v1 https://token:${{ secrets.SHARED_ACTION_PAT }}@git.example.com/user-a/shared-action.git .gitea/actions/shared-action

    - name: Run Action
      uses: ./.gitea/actions/shared-action
      with:
        # action inputs...
```
*(Add `.gitea/actions/` to `.gitignore` to keep cloned actions untracked).*

**Why this works:**
* `git clone` inside a `run:` step bypasses `act_runner`'s automatic token injection and clones anonymously.
* `act_runner` reads local actions (`uses: ./.gitea/actions/...`) dynamically at step execution time without calling the Gitea API.

---

## Proposed Fix

1. **Gitea Side:** In `githttp.go` (and `CheckRepoScopedToken`), if a repository is **public** and the requested action is a read-only pull (`git-upload-pack`), Gitea should not deny access simply because the supplied `GITEA_TOKEN` is scoped to a different repository. An authenticated user/token should never have fewer permissions than an anonymous guest.
2. **`act_runner` Side:** Support either attempting an unauthenticated clone fallback if an authenticated clone returns 404/401 on an action URL, or checking if the host is a public Git remote before injecting `github.Token`.

### Gitea Version

1.27.3

### What happened?

Global git pull/clone instant disconnect (Broken Pipe) following Web UI Merge — Push works, local clone works

## Environment

* Gitea Version: 1.24.6 (Prod mode)
* Git Version (Server): 2.49.1 (Linux)
* Database Backend: SQLite
* Deployment: Docker Swarm (Internal overlay networking tested)

## The Problem / Symptoms

Following a branch merge completed via the Gitea Web UI, a global anomaly has triggered across all repositories on the instance:

   1. git push works perfectly across all repositories.
   2. git pull / git clone fails instantly (within 2ms) across both SSH and HTTPS channels universally.
   3. Local clones work flawlessly: Running git clone /data/... directly from inside the container filesystem works with zero errors. Running git-upload-pack . manually on the bare repository returns clean protocol refs.

## Server-Side Behavior (gitea.log)

When a client attempts a pull, the Gitea routing engine successfully authorizes the request and updates the keys. It writes a 200 OK response and logs absolutely zero errors, warnings, or panic traces:

2026/09/11 19:27:11 HTTPRequest [I] router: completed GET /api/internal/serv/command/60/xWave/ai-server?mode=1&verb=git-upload-pack for 10.0.0.7:0, 200 OK in 1.5ms @ private/serv.go:79(private.ServCommand)
2026/09/11 19:27:11 HTTPRequest [I] router: completed POST /api/internal/ssh/60/update/316 for 10.0.0.7:0, 200 OK in 5.5ms @ private/key.go:16(private.UpdatePublicKeyInRepo)

## Client-Side Behavior (ssh -vvv git pull)

Immediately after Gitea processes the internal validation, the container drops the socket connection cleanly, causing the client to encounter a Broken pipe right when opening the standard read buffer:

debug1: channel 0: setting env GIT_PROTOCOL = "version=2"
debug2: channel 0: request env confirm 0
debug3: send packet: type 98
debug1: Sending command: git-upload-pack '/xWave/ai-server.git'
debug2: channel 0: request exec confirm 1
debug3: send packet: type 98
debug2: exec request accepted on channel 0
debug2: channel 0: read failed rfd 6 maxlen 32768: Broken pipe
debug2: channel 0: read failed
debug2: chan_shutdown_read: channel 0: (i0 o0 sock -1 wfd 4 efd 6 [write])
fatal: early EOF
fatal: fetch-pack: invalid index-pack output
Killed by signal 15.

## Steps Taken / Diagnostics Verified

* No Database Locks: Confirmed that gitea.db has no active WAL or journal locks (wal_checkpoint completed, no temporary files present).
* No Filesystem Corruption: git fsck runs completely clean across the repositories.
* No File Permissions Changes: Repository structures and reference files are intact (git:git 644).
* Isolated Networking: The issue reproduces identically from a testing container connected directly to the same internal Docker overlay network, ruling out external reverse proxies or host-level firewalls.

It appears that a state change triggered during the Web UI merge has placed Gitea's internal Go orchestration layer or process execution flow into a deadlock or routing loop specifically for outbound data streams (git-upload-pack), while leaving the inbound path (git-receive-pack) completely unaffected.

* Gitea Version: 1.24.6 (Prod mode)
* Git Version (Server): 2.49.1 (Linux)

   2. git pull / git clone fails instantly (within 2ms) across both SSH and HTTPS channels universally.
   3. Local clones work flawlessly: Running git clone /data/... directly from inside the container filesystem works with zero errors. Running git-upload-pack . manually on the bare repository returns clean protocol refs.

### What problem would this solve?

At the moment it seems like the last commit, on any branch, goes on to the left-most line on the Commit Graph display, working its way right in date order of commits on other branches.

It can be unnecessarily hard to find the Default branch and can be quite confusing.


### What do you propose?

Further to #36825 (and this may render that request obsolete), would it be possible to have a repository option that fixed the Default branch on the left hand side of the display on the Commit Graph page and which prevented other branches from displaying in a continuation of that line? i.e. all branches always go on a separate line.

Implementing this would aid usability.

### What problem would this solve?

Workflow files that have a `on: workflow_call:` only are shown in the list of workflows in the actions tab.
As these will never run - the history will be empty forever.

See also https://gitea.com/gitea/runner/issues/1239

### What do you propose?

I suggest to hide workflow files (even if placed in `.gitea/workflows`) from the list as there will never run.
Advantage: the workflow list becomes more clean

### What problem would this solve?

Hi maintainers — thank you for Gitea.

We maintain a small fork for better mobile use, and recently landed two independent changes there for our own needs. They seem generally useful, so I wanted to ask whether you would like them upstreamed. If not, that is completely fine — please just close this issue.

### 1. Fix: Mobile Safari input focus zoom
Mobile Safari zooms focused form controls when the computed font-size is below 16px. We raise shared form controls to 16px under the existing mobile breakpoint, without disabling viewport zoom.

- Commit: https://github.com/b4moss/gitea/commit/21fe9c606d402b7f8882321ea41f654261ceb41e

### 2. Enhance: make `site-manifest.json` installable (minimal PWA)
Gitea already serves a site manifest, but Chromium installability is weak without `display` / icon sizing. We add `display: "standalone"`, `theme_color`, and a 192×192 PNG icon so the site can be installed without a Service Worker.

Out of scope on purpose: offline support, and we are **not** proposing to bring back a caching Service Worker.

We are aware that the Gitea team previously stepped away from a fuller PWA direction (including removing the Service Worker). We do **not** claim to know whether this minimal manifest-only change fits that earlier plan or current product direction. If you decide it does not belong upstream for that reason, we fully respect that judgment.

- Commit: https://github.com/b4moss/gitea/commit/177b2dd788771d9e210c1387149ed445c611115f

### What do you propose?


### Proposed contribution shape
If useful, I would open **two separate PRs** (one per change) and keep this single issue as the discussion / tracking place. Happy to split into two issues instead if you prefer.

### Questions
1. Would either or both of these be welcome upstream?
2. Is **one issue + two PRs** an acceptable shape, or would you rather we do something different?

Again: these were built for our fork. We are glad to share if they fit the project; if they do not, closing this issue is perfectly OK. Thanks for your time.

### Gitea Version

main (ea91028); the docs page is the current one on docs.gitea.com.

### What happened?

For the `pull_request_review_approved`, `pull_request_review_rejected` and `pull_request_review_comment` webhooks, the docs say `review.type` is `approved`, `rejected` or `comment` (`docs/usage/repository/webhooks.md` in gitea/docs), and the `ReviewPayload.Type` comment in `modules/structs/hook.go` says the same.

The payload carries the full event name instead. `PullRequestReview` in `services/webhook/notifier.go` sets `Type: string(reviewHookType)`, and `reviewHookType` is one of the `HookEventPullRequestReview*` constants, so an approval arrives as `"type": "pull_request_review_approved"`. The Actions notifier in `services/actions/notifier.go` does the same.

A consumer that follows the docs and matches on `approved` never matches. Integrations that exist today already read the full names, so bringing the docs in line with the payload looks safer than changing the payload. The docs page and the struct comment both need the change.

### How are you running Gitea?

Read from the source on main; it doesn't depend on the install.

### What problem would this solve?

## 📝 Context & Motivation

Many teams and enterprises adopting Gitea face a common structural bottleneck: the organization structure is completely flat. While Gitea is widely appreciated for its lightweight design and speed, the lack of hierarchical **Repo Grouping / Subgroups** under organizations makes it difficult to scale for large teams, microservice architectures, or multi-department setups.

This has been a long-standing request within the community (frequently discussed in older threads like Issue #1872 and related feature requests).

## ❓ Questions for Maintainers & Core Contributors

As the project evolves, we would love to get an update on the current stance and roadmap regarding this feature:

1. **Current Status:** Is there an active RFC, design proposal, or branch working on hierarchical organization groups / subgroups?
2. **Architectural Roadmap:** What are the primary technical blockers preventing this implementation? (e.g., URL routing changes, Git path storage, or permission inheritance models like Team ACLs)?
3. **Community Contribution:** If this is currently unassigned or planned for a later milestone, is the core team open to community contributions or design proposals for this feature? If so, is there an existing preferred architectural direction?

Any insights, updates, or pointers to ongoing discussions would be greatly appreciated by the community!

### What do you propose?

To introduce repo grouping with minimal disruption, we propose an incremental database-first approach: introducing a dedicated `repo_groups` table with self-referencing parent IDs to establish structural foundations. This allows for an initial phase of virtual grouping and dashboard filtering while keeping existing repository routes intact, before gradually layering on hierarchical URL routing and team permission inheritance as the feature matures.

### What problem would this solve?

## Description

In a setup with no auto-registration (`oauth2_client.ENABLE_AUTO_REGISTRATION=false`)
where local accounts are pre-provisioned and then linked to an OIDC provider via the
`/user/link_account` flow, there's no clean way to disable the local password (and
personal access token) authentication for a linked user while keeping their OIDC
session fully functional.

## What I tried

1. **Changing "Authentication Source" via the admin edit-user page** to the OAuth2
   source: has no effect on local password auth. `services/auth/source/db/authenticate.go`'s
   `Authenticate()` never checks `user.LoginType`/`LoginSource`, only
   `user.IsPasswordSet()` and `user.ProhibitLogin`. Verified empirically: local
   password login and Basic-Auth API calls both kept working (HTTP 200) after the
   switch.

2. **`oauth2_client.ACCOUNT_LINKING = auto`**: per the config cheat sheet this
   "automatically link[s] with existing accounts", but reading
   `routers/web/auth/oauth.go`'s `SignInOAuthCallback`, the `OAuth2AccountLinkingDisabled`
   check only applies inside the auto-*registration* branch (creating a brand new
   user). With auto-registration off, every first-time OIDC login with no prior
   `external_login_user` row always falls through to `showLinkingLogin()`
   regardless of this setting - so it doesn't affect our scenario at all.

3. **`user.ProhibitLogin = true`** (via `PATCH /api/v1/admin/users/{username}`):
   this DOES block local password/Basic-Auth (confirmed in
   `services/auth/source/db/authenticate.go`), and `oAuth2UserLoginCallback`/
   `handleOAuth2SignIn` in `routers/web/auth/oauth.go` don't check it - so the
   initial OAuth2 lookup/redirect isn't blocked. However, it ALSO blocks
   **personal access token** authentication entirely (empirically verified: a
   previously-working PAT started returning 403 as soon as `ProhibitLogin` was
   set, and went back to 200 immediately after unsetting it). This makes it
   unusable for a user who also needs API/git-over-HTTPS access via a token.

### What do you propose?

I'd like to propose a scoped variant of `ProhibitLogin` that only blocks
password/PAT authentication, leaving OIDC/OAuth2 sign-in untouched.

Concretely: a new user-level flag, e.g. `ProhibitLocalLogin` (or reusing
`ProhibitLogin` but adding a `LoginSource`-aware check), that is:

- checked in `services/auth/source/db/authenticate.go`'s `Authenticate()`
  (same place `ProhibitLogin` is checked today) - blocks the local password path;
- checked in whatever auth.Method validates personal access tokens - blocks PAT/API-token auth;
- **not** checked in `routers/web/auth/oauth.go` (`oAuth2UserLoginCallback`,
  `handleOAuth2SignIn`) - OIDC sign-in and the resulting session keep working exactly
  as today.

This would let an admin fully commit a user to SSO-only access (no password,
no long-lived token that could leak and bypass the identity provider's own
MFA/conditional-access policies) without disabling the account outright.

A simpler alternative that would also solve this: let `ProhibitLogin` be scoped
per login source (e.g. "prohibit login via source X") instead of global, since
in our case the account already has both a local source (id 0) and a linked
external source (the OIDC one) - prohibiting only source 0 would achieve the
same result without touching PAT/OAuth2 auth paths that don't belong to a
specific "source" in the same sense.

body_text:
Gitea 28.0.0’s bot administration is a welcome improvement. However, the bot-edit form still exposes settings whose meaning is unclear for noninteractive accounts.

Examples:

- **“Prohibit login”** appears redundant because bots already cannot sign in interactively. In practice, it also blocks token/API authentication. An administrator could enable it intending to prevent browser login and unintentionally disable automation.
- **Email remains required and unique**, although bots receive no email. The form does not explain why an address is needed.
- **Language, location, website and avatar settings** remain alongside operational permissions without distinguishing optional profile metadata from settings affecting automation.

This is not a request to remove legitimate bot capabilities. Repository-creation limits and permissions can be meaningful for automation accounts.

## Suggested improvements

- Use bot-specific wording such as **“Disable bot access, including API tokens”** for the prohibit-login control.
- Explain that Bot type already prevents interactive sign-in.
- Explain the email requirement and link to the remaining work tracked in #21704.
- Group optional profile fields separately from authentication and authorization controls.
- Surface incompatible legacy account states, such as a pending password-change requirement.

Related: #13044 and #38966.

### What problem would this solve?

Currently if you use a repository template to create a new repository, actions do not run on the first commit (the commit creating the repository). If you wish to use actions to initialise the repository in ways not possible using the template, then you must manually run actions. 

This does not match the behaviour in GitHub. The behaviour is described here: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/52965

I also validated this behaviour in GitHub myself:
- Template: [MrMeeb/actions-test-template](https://github.com/MrMeeb/actions-test-template)
- Cloned repo: [MrMeeb/actions-test-template-clone](https://github.com/MrMeeb/actions-test-template-clone)

In there I included a workflow with the `push` trigger. As soon as I used the template to create the repo, the action ran on the new repo. 

Doing the same on Gitea (28.0.0, runner 4.1.0) does not cause a run. I need to manually trigger it using `workflow_dispatch`

### What do you propose?

Mirror the GitHub behaviour - the first commit of the repo is able to trigger actions

body_text: ### What problem would this solve? Today with external CI, there is no distinction between pending builds and running builds. See state in REST API [/repos/{owner}/{repo}/statuses/{sha}](https://docs.gitea.com/api/1.27/operations/repo-create-status/#request-body) But when using gitea action we see a nice animation for running builds. If the value "running" is set in `state`, there is no icons: I tried with "in_progress" but the server then return error code 500. ### What do you propose? Add officially value "running" for `state` in rest request [/repos/{owner}/{repo}/statuses/{sha}](https://docs.gitea.com/api/1.27/operations/repo-create-status/#request-body) that show on the check area of pull requests.

body_text:
Runs triggered by `workflow_dispatch` execute against a resolved commit SHA, but Gitea never creates a commit status for them. The run appears in the Actions tab only; the commit itself shows no indication that a workflow ran on it.

From reading `services/actions/commit_status.go`, the status handler switches on the triggering event and only handles push, the `pull_request*` family and a few others. All other events, including `workflow_dispatch` and `schedule`, fall through to the `default` case, which returns `nil`, so no status is created. Other events have been added to this switch over time (e.g. `pull_request_review` in #36589), so this seems to be a gap rather than a deliberate exclusion.

**Expected behavior (GitHub parity):**
On GitHub, dispatched runs are recorded against the head SHA and show up in the commit's checks. They are *not* linked to pull requests: only `push` and the `pull_request*` events update PR check information. A manual run therefore documents itself on the commit without affecting PR merge checks.

**Proposal:**
- Create commit statuses for `workflow_dispatch` runs on `run.CommitSHA`, using the existing context format, e.g. `ci / e2e (workflow_dispatch)`.
- Optionally do the same for `schedule`, or make it configurable, since scheduled runs re-stamp the default branch tip repeatedly.

**Points to consider:**
- *Required status checks:* because the event name is part of the context, a dispatch status wouldn't match protection patterns like `ci / e2e (pull_request)`. But broad globs (e.g. `ci / e2e*`) would match. Anyone with permission to dispatch could then satisfy or override a required check, possibly with inputs that skip work. It might be worth excluding non-code events from required-check evaluation, or at least documenting this.
- *Inputs:* two dispatched runs on the same SHA can test different things depending on inputs. The latest one would win for that context.

**Use case:**
We use manually dispatched workflows (e.g. long-running E2E suites, release verification) and want their result visible on the commit they ran against. Today the only workaround is calling `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/statuses/{sha}` from within the workflow with a separate token.

### Gitea Version

28.0.0
