### Proposal Details

I propose adding a `ReadDir` method to `*os.Root`:

```go
package os

// ReadDir reads the named directory in the root,
// returning all its directory entries sorted by filename.
// See [ReadDir] for more details.
func (r *Root) ReadDir(name string) ([]DirEntry, error)
```

This is a convenience method, like `Root.ReadFile` and `Root.WriteFile` (#73126). I propose adding it because:

1. `os.ReadDir` is a useful convenience function, and it is useful to have an equivalent that works directly with `os.Root`.
2. The `io/fs` package includes both `ReadDir` and the `ReadDirFS` interface, suggesting that directory listing is core filesystem functionality.
3. `fs.ReadDir(r.FS(), name)` uses `io/fs` path syntax, while methods on `Root` accept native `os` path syntax.

This method was considered during the original `Root` proposal and explicitly left as a possible follow-up (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/67002#issuecomment-2430411464).

This gap has also appeared in practice: [apko](https://github.com/chainguard-dev/apko/blob/38315bf3765f/pkg/apk/fs/rwosfs.go#L481-L499) explicitly notes that `*os.Root` does not expose `ReadDir` and works around it using `Root.Open` followed by `File.ReadDir`.

Several interpreters for dynamic languages are implemented in Go, such as [starlark-go](https://pkg.go.dev/go.starlark.net/starlark), [go-lua](https://github.com/Shopify/go-lua), [ivy](https://github.com/robpike/ivy), [goawk](https://github.com/benhoyt/goawk), and [many others](https://awesome-go.com/embeddable-scripting-languages/). In all such projects, there comes a time when the users start to ask for profiling tools. The interpreter maintainer has essentially no way to build high-quality implementations of these tools, because (a) they require direct integration into the runtime and so cannot be implemented in application code, and (b) a profile of an interpreter is an inextricable mix of operations in two languages--host (Go) and target--so a profile of just the target language is incomplete.

Fortunately the Go runtime/pprof package provides high-quality implementations of profilers for many resources including CPU, allocation, and so on. This proposal seeks to open them up to support dynamic languages.

The basic problem is that profiling an interpreter produces a profile that attributes much of the the resource cost of each target language function to the interpreter's general "eval" function, which is implemented in Go, when the user really wants to know which target language function is being evaluated. The solution (or vague outline of a solution) we propose here is a mechanism to allow applications to register with the runtime certain "eval" functions, marking them as special, so that when the profiler's stack unwinder encounters them, it should instead report a "virtual frame" whose (function name, file name, line number) triple is provided by the interpreter.

For this to work, there needs to be a local variable (or perhaps multiple variables) inside the eval function from which the triple can be derived, and the unwinder needs to be able to find it reliably, even in a handler for an async signal such as SIGPROF. This means the compiler must be instructed to place the variable somewhere predictable, such as a particular stack slot, and not to optimize its liveness. We propose a compiler annotation `//go:virtualframe fr` preceding the function to identify the variable `fr`. Assume for now that the variable is a pointer.  The compiler must also force its referent to escape to the heap, since the unwinder will need to copy the pointer (or a derived one) later and won't be able to insert a write barrier.

The registration mechanism mentioned above also provides two expressions and a callback function (described later). The two expressions are applied to the value of the pointer `fr`. The first computes a static part, a pointer, which we'll call "code"; the second computes a dynamic part, an integer, which we'll call "pc". This matches the design of many interpreters, which represent each function as a whole by a data structure, and use some kind of index for the current instruction, bytecode, or subexpression that is currently being evaluated. But in principle we could support an arbitrary number of pointers or integers, whatever is needed to match the design of a wide range of interpreters.

These expressions, effectively functions from the `fr` variable to its "code" and "pc" subcomponents, cannot be ordinary Go functions or methods, because they must be safe to execute by the unwinder in async signal handler context. Therefore they are expressed in a restricted sublanguage that can be safely evaluated by the unwinder.  We anticipate expressions such as `x.(*T).f[i]`, that chase pointers, index arrays, load fields, and type-assert interfaces, but nothing more. (Even type assertions may be tricky.) These expressions are constructed in AST form directly by the client, and compile to a tiny bytecode language interpreted by the unwinder, similar to a BPF or DWARF program. The design space here is pretty enormous. I chose to use a type-safe generic "builder pattern" for constructing the expressions; see the virtualframe.go link below.

The unwinder evaluates these two (or more) expressions, then stashes their values (pointers or integers) in the profile event circular buffer. (We cannot simply save the value of the fr variable itself in the profile buffer as it refers to time-varying state.) The GC needs to be taught to treat these buffered pointers as heap edges.  Shortly after, the runtime's pprof writer (in ordinary goroutine context) calls the interpreter-provided callback function to convert the (code, pc) values into the (function name, file name, line number) triple required by the profile. This gives the interpreter plenty of latitude to express this conversion. It is worth noting that this design does slightly prolong the lifetime of the "code" pointers, potentially perturbing the GC dynamics of the program being profiled, but the effect is expected to be small.

I've built (assisted by an LLM) a sketch of a working prototype of the compiler, runtime, and interpreter changes in the following CLs:

- cmd/compile: https://go.dev/cl/831624
- runtime/pprof: https://go.dev/cl/831625
- Starlark interpreter: https://github.com/google/starlark-go/pull/659 (see [virtualframe.go](https://github.com/google/starlark-go/blob/pprof-virtual-frame/starlark/virtualframe.go))

FWIW, the go-lua interpreter would need two `//go:virtualframe` variables, the `f` and `i` found [here](https://github.com/Shopify/go-lua/blob/main/vm.go#L942-L945), a slight design tweak. Other interpreters may need more virtualframe variables, or more subexpressions derived from them using the bytecode expression mechanism.

{"repository": "golang/go", "task_candidate_id": 5970, "repository_id": 108, "issue_number": 81529, "github_issue_id": 5455872103, "html_url": "https://github.com/golang/go/issues/81529", "created_at": "2026-09-15T00:04:57+00:00", "author_association": null, "title": "runtime/pprof: support dynamic languages with "virtual frames"", "body_text": "Several interpreters for dynamic languages are implemented in Go, such as [starlark-go](https://pkg.go.dev/go.starlark.net/starlark), [go-lua](https://github.com/Shopify/go-lua), [ivy](https://github.com/robpike/ivy), [goawk](https://github.com/benhoyt/goawk), and [many others](https://awesome-go.com/embeddable-scripting-languages/). In all such projects, there comes a time when the users start to ask for profiling tools. The interpreter maintainer has essentially no way to build high-quality implementations of these tools, because (a) they require direct integration into the runtime and so cannot be implemented in application code, and (b) a profile of an interpreter is an inextricable mix of operations in two languages--host (Go) and target--so a profile of just the target language is incomplete.

Fortunately the Go runtime/pprof package provides high-quality implementations of profilers for many resources including CPU, allocation, and so on. This proposal seeks to open them up to support dynamic languages.

The basic problem is that profiling an interpreter produces a profile that attributes much of the the resource cost of each target language function to the interpreter's general "eval" function, which is implemented in Go, when the user really wants to know which target language function is being evaluated. The solution (or vague outline of a solution) we propose here is a mechanism to allow applications to register with the runtime certain "eval" functions, marking them as special, so that when the profiler's stack unwinder encounters them, it should instead report a "virtual frame" whose (function name, file name, line number) triple is provided by the interpreter.

For this to work, there needs to be a local variable (or perhaps multiple variables) inside the eval function from which the triple can be derived, and the unwinder needs to be able to find it reliably, even in a handler for an async signal such as SIGPROF. This means the compiler must be instructed to place the variable somewhere predictable, such as a particular stack slot, and not to optimize its liveness. We propose a compiler annotation `//go:virtualframe fr` preceding the function to identify the variable `fr`. Assume for now that the variable is a pointer.  The compiler must also force its referent to escape to the heap, since the unwinder will need to copy the pointer (or a derived one) later and won't be able to insert a write barrier.

The registration mechanism mentioned above also provides two expressions and a callback function (described later). The two expressions are applied to the value of the pointer `fr`. The first computes a static part, a pointer, which we'll call "code"; the second computes a dynamic part, an integer, which we'll call "pc". This matches the design of many interpreters, which represent each function as a whole by a data structure, and use some kind of index for the current instruction, bytecode, or subexpression that is currently being evaluated. But in principle we could support an arbitrary number of pointers or integers, whatever is needed to match the design of a wide range of interpreters.

These expressions, effectively functions from the `fr` variable to its "code" and "pc" subcomponents, cannot be ordinary Go functions or methods, because they must be safe to execute by the unwinder in async signal handler context. Therefore they are expressed in a restricted sublanguage that can be safely evaluated by the unwinder.  We anticipate expressions such as `x.(*T).f[i]`, that chase pointers, index arrays, load fields, and type-assert interfaces, but nothing more. (Even type assertions may be tricky.) These expressions are constructed in AST form directly by the client, and compile to a tiny bytecode language interpreted by the unwinder, similar to a BPF or DWARF program. The design space here is pretty enormous. I chose to use a type-safe generic "builder pattern" for constructing the expressions; see the virtualframe.go link below.

The unwinder evaluates these two (or more) expressions, then stashes their values (pointers or integers) in the profile event circular buffer. (We cannot simply save the value of the fr variable itself in the profile buffer as it refers to time-varying state.) The GC needs to be taught to treat these buffered pointers as heap edges.  Shortly after, the runtime's pprof writer (in ordinary goroutine context) calls the interpreter-provided callback function to convert the (code, pc) values into the (function name, file name, line number) triple required by the profile. This gives the interpreter plenty of latitude to express this conversion. It is worth noting that this design does slightly prolong the lifetime of the "code" pointers, potentially perturbing the GC dynamics of the program being profiled, but the effect is expected to be small.

I've built (assisted by an LLM) a sketch of a working prototype of the compiler, runtime, and interpreter changes in the following CLs:

- cmd/compile: https://go.dev/cl/831624
- runtime/pprof: https://go.dev/cl/831625
- Starlark interpreter: https://github.com/google/starlark-go/pull/659 (see [virtualframe.go](https://github.com/google/starlark-go/blob/pprof-virtual-frame/starlark/virtualframe.go))

FWIW, the go-lua interpreter would need two `//go:virtualframe` variables, the `f` and `i` found [here](https://github.com/Shopify/go-lua/blob/main/vm.go#L942-L945), a slight design tweak. Other interpreters may need more virtualframe variables, or more subexpressions derived from them using the bytecode expression mechanism.

body_text:
Lifted from the original report:

```
`knownhosts.Line` performs no validation or escaping on the addresses it is
given, so an address containing a newline causes it to return several lines
rather than one. Because the documented use of `Line` is to append its result
to a `known_hosts` file, a caller that passes an attacker-influenced address
writes an attacker-chosen entry into that file.

Injecting `@cert-authority * <attacker CA>` installs a wildcard certificate
authority, after which `knownhosts.New` accepts an attacker-signed host
certificate for **any** host, including hosts that
never appeared in the file.
```

This was originally reported as http://b/548517658 and triaged as not
a vulnerability.

body_text:
Lifted from the original report:

````
`[golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts`](http://golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts%60)
<http://golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts> performs byte-exact pattern
matching when evaluating wildcard and negation entries in `known_hosts`.
DNS hostnames are case-insensitive (RFC 4343), but `wildcardMatch`
(knownhosts.go line 78) and `hostPattern.match` (line 109) compare pattern
bytes directly against the connection address bytes, with no DNS case
normalization applied before the comparison. `knownhosts.Normalize` (line
427) also preserves the case of the hostname it receives.

With this `known_hosts` policy:

```
@cert-authority *.[example.com](http://example.com/),![blocked.example.com](http://blocked.example.com/) <CA public key>
```
````

This was originally reported as http://b/521350695 and triaged as not
a vulnerability.

````
`[golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts`](http://golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts%60)
<http://golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts> performs byte-exact pattern
matching when evaluating wildcard and negation entries in `known_hosts`.
DNS hostnames are case-insensitive (RFC 4343), but `wildcardMatch`
(knownhosts.go line 78) and `hostPattern.match` (line 109) compare pattern
bytes directly against the connection address bytes, with no DNS case
normalization applied before the comparison. `knownhosts.Normalize` (line
427) also preserves the case of the hostname it receives.

With this `known_hosts` policy:

```
@cert-authority *.[example.com](http://example.com/),![blocked.example.com](http://blocked.example.com/) <CA public key>
```
````

### What did you do?

I'm using flate to compress individial messages in a streaming protocol. After switching from 1.26 to 1.27 I've noticed that if two identical messages are sent with another short message between, the second copy of the message does not use a reference to the first copy and is sent in full instead.

In 1.26 this behaviour is only observed on compression level 1, in 1.27 -- on levels 1-6 inclusive.
Reproducing code: https://go.dev/play/p/9V1TyhjEzS6

Note that if there is no intermediate message or if there is no Flush() call after that intermediate message is sent, it works as expected.

This may be an acceptable behaviour in general, but in my case this is a very typical traffic pattern. With the new version I'll have to raise the compression level to 7 which incurs a significant CPU and memory penalty.

```
Package/API: encoding/json, json.Indent(dst *bytes.Buffer, src []byte,
prefix, indent string)
Location: src/encoding/json/v2_indent.go:86,109,130 (JSONv2 baseline,
e62d3e6e89; go1.25+)

Summary: appendIndent emits placeholder spaces that a deferred closure
rewrites over the produced buffer. That rewrite loop makes no progress when
indent is the empty string (copy(spaces, "") == 0), so the loop never
terminates. Trigger: indent == "" together with a non-whitespace prefix and
trailing whitespace in src (both legal). Four bytes of valid JSON ("1\n ",
prefix ">", indent "") spin a goroutine forever.
```

body_text:
Lifted from the original report:

```
I found a reproducible memory-exhaustion issue in net/http/fcgi while
looking at multiplexed request handling. It requires direct access to the
raw FastCGI socket. I could not reach it through the normal nginx HTTP
frontend I tested.

An FCGI_BEGIN_REQUEST record is 16 bytes. For every new request ID,
net/http/fcgi creates a request containing an inline 1,024-byte buffer and
stores it in the connection's request map:

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/fdcd66bb544d230a7eb0c2512e9e7a6ab191388b/src/net/http/fcgi/child.go#L22-L44

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/fdcd66bb544d230a7eb0c2512e9e7a6ab191388b/src/net/http/fcgi/child.go#L193-L218

If the client keeps the connection open and sends neither an empty STDIN
record nor ABORT_REQUEST, those entries remain allocated. The HTTP handler
is never reached.
```

This was originally reported as http://b/561524698 and triaged as
not a security issue.

```
I found a reproducible memory-exhaustion issue in net/http/fcgi while
looking at multiplexed request handling. It requires direct access to the
raw FastCGI socket. I could not reach it through the normal nginx HTTP
frontend I tested.

An FCGI_BEGIN_REQUEST record is 16 bytes. For every new request ID,
net/http/fcgi creates a request containing an inline 1,024-byte buffer and
stores it in the connection's request map:

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/fdcd66bb544d230a7eb0c2512e9e7a6ab191388b/src/net/http/fcgi/child.go#L22-L44

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/fdcd66bb544d230a7eb0c2512e9e7a6ab191388b/src/net/http/fcgi/child.go#L193-L218

If the client keeps the connection open and sends neither an empty STDIN
record nor ABORT_REQUEST, those entries remain allocated. The HTTP handler
is never reached.
```

```
a pre-conversion policy check to collapse to a protected DNS name.

[example.com](http://example.com/). and [example.com](http://example.com/) identify the same absolute DNS name. The
package-level ToUnicode and ToASCII functions, together with the
corresponding Lookup methods, all return the canonicalized value without an
error.
```

Lifted from the original report:

```
[golang.org/x/text/secure/precis](http://golang.org/x/text/secure/precis) implements RFC 8264 PRECIS, a framework
specifically designed to make string handling (usernames, nicknames,
passwords, identifiers) safe against spoofing, comparison confusion, and
invalid input. The package exposes two parallel ways to apply a Profile's
rules to a string:

1. The buffer-based methods Profile.String, Profile.Bytes, Profile.Append,
   Profile.Compare, Profile.CompareKey -- all backed by the internal
   enforce() function in profile.go.
2. The streaming transform.Transformer returned by Profile.NewTransformer()
   -- meant to perform "the PRECIS preparation and enforcement steps" (per
   its own doc comment) so it can be used with
transform.NewReader/NewWriter,
   transform.String, transform.Bytes, or the Transformer's own
   .String()/.Bytes() convenience methods.

These two paths are not equivalent. NewTransformer()'s transform chain never
enforces:

- The Disallow() option (and therefore NewRestrictedProfile(), the package's
  own documented mechanism for adding application-specific character
  restrictions on top of a base profile).
- The DisallowEmpty option (used by the built-in Nickname and OpaqueString
  profiles).
```


### What did you do?

Ran a cgo-linked binary (cgo is pulled in transitively via github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/internal/dlopen, not via direct import "C" in our own code) repeatedly under normal load. The binary is short-lived (a CLI subcommand that runs, does some work, and exits). No unusual rlimits, cgroup limits, or memory pressure at time of failure — see below.

### What did you see happen?

An intermittent, unrecoverable abort during runtime startup, before main() is ever reached:

runtime/cgo: pthread_create failed: Resource temporarily unavailable
SIGABRT: abort

goroutine 1 [running, locked to thread]:
runtime.systemstack_switch()
runtime.newm1(...)
runtime.newm(...)
runtime.startTemplateThread()
runtime.main()

In other captures the failure instead lands slightly later, during the GC-helper goroutine/thread spin-up (still pre-main()), sometimes printing runtime/cgo: pthread_create failed twice in a row before the abort, and in one capture as fatal error: runtime: cannot allocate memory via runtime.(*mheap).allocSpan → runtime.persistentalloc instead of the cgo message.

We ruled out every resource ceiling we could find before concluding this was a runtime issue rather than an environment one, all clean/unremarkable at the moment of failure:

RLIMIT_AS (soft 1GiB, hard unlimited), RLIMIT_NPROC (limit 23454, ~16 threads in use for the whole UID)
cgroup v2 memory.max unlimited at every level in the hierarchy; memory.events' max/oom/oom_kill counters all 0
System-wide /proc/meminfo: Committed_AS flat around 2.65GB against a 9.1GB CommitLimit; MemAvailable steady ~4.1GB
vm.max_map_count at the 65530 default; single NUMA node, /proc/buddyinfo unremarkable
SELinux Permissive (no relevant AVC denials); VMware balloon driver at 0MB; vmstat showing an idle system (90–100% idle CPU, no swap/disk I/O) at time of failure

An strace -f on the parent process showed clone3() succeeding every time; widening the trace to include mmap/mprotect/brk caught a real mmap(NULL, 262144, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) returning -1 ENOMEM for a just-clone3()'d thread immediately before one of the aborts — i.e. pthread_create's internal stack allocation fails at the mmap() step itself, not at clone3(), despite nothing above showing pressure.

Failure rate was workload-dependent — frequent on a high-invocation-frequency code path, rare on a low-frequency one using identical code and environment — which reads more like a narrow timing window in the runtime's startup thread-creation sequence than a hard resource limit. Pinning the toolchain to go1.25.9 eliminated the failure entirely across 10 consecutive runs of a workload that previously failed on most attempts under 1.26.5/1.26.7.

### What did you expect to see?

The process starts and runs normally, as it does under go1.25.9 and as it does most of the time even under go1.26.x.

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?

Crashes:
```
go1.26.8
```

Does not crash — same source, same environment, only the build toolchain changed:
```
go1.25.14
```

### What operating system and processor architecture are you using (`go env GOOS GOARCH`)?

```
GOOS=linux
GOARCH=amd64
```

Container OS: Bottlerocket OS 1.65.0 (aws-k8s-1.35), containerd 2.2.7, cgroup v2.
Host kernel: `6.12.103` — crashes.
Same container image, same binary, run on a host kernel `6.12.94` (Bottlerocket 1.64.0, otherwise
identical AMI family) — does **not** crash. This is the only environment variable that reproducibly
flips the outcome (see "Isolation" below).

Reproduced on AWS EC2 (all `amd64`, all crash on kernel 6.12.103): `c8i-flex.2xlarge` (Intel),
`m7i-flex.2xlarge` (Intel), `c6a.2xlarge` (AMD) — so it isn't CPU-vendor-specific.

### What did you do?

A small, otherwise-idle internal Go service (a Kubernetes-in-cluster HTTP API server, low request
volume) started crash-looping in production after its EKS nodegroup rolled from Bottlerocket 1.64.0
(kernel 6.12.94) to 1.65.0 (kernel 6.12.103). Isolated it with a controlled A/B, one variable changed
at a time, using throwaway Kubernetes pods pinned to specific nodes via `nodeName`:

1. Same image, 3 different nodes spanning Intel and AMD instance families, all on kernel 6.12.103
   → crashes every time, ruling out CPU vendor/family.
2. Same image, a node on kernel 6.12.94 (older Bottlerocket) → clean for 5.5+ minutes (well past
   every crash window seen elsewhere), ruling out resource limits / GOMAXPROCS / anything about the
   binary itself and isolating the kernel version.
3. Rebuilt the identical source with `golang:1.25-alpine` instead of `golang:1.26-alpine` as the
   Docker build base, ran it on the exact node that had just crashed twice under 1.26 → clean for
   5.5+ minutes.

Build command (both variants):
```
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' -o /app .
```
No `GOMAXPROCS`/`GOMEMLIMIT` env vars set; no CGO; a small program that does routine
`crypto/x509`/`net/http` work (parses a CA bundle into an `x509.CertPool` via `AppendCertsFromPEM`
at startup for a couple of TLS clients) and otherwise sits mostly idle serving occasional HTTP

body_text:
Some packages need to be aliased frequently as they have a name you would rather use as a variable, collide with another package you need to import, or for better clarity at usage sites. goimports works great at long as you're not dealing with any of those cases. When you are, there are some rough edges, as you need to
- repeat the aliasing in each file
- add the alias back after temporarily not using it in a file caused it to be removed
- stay consistent across a project / meet an internal style guide

If goimports knew that, for example, I always wanted crypto/rand aliased to cryptorand it could import math/rand safely if I write `var _ = rand.Int` and know to add the appropriately aliased import for crypto/rand when I write `cryptorand.Text()`.

Adding configuration is distasteful but it would allow goimports to know about these alias preferences ahead of time and make it one more thing that goimports allows us to stop thinking about. I have no particular preferences for the syntax or location of this config file.

Some recent comments about goimports and aliased imports:
- https://github.com/golang/go/issues/80590#issuecomment-5718218463
- https://github.com/golang/go/issues/81581#issuecomment-5720115911

### What did you do?

I tested the keyboard navigation on the current A Tour of Go at:

https://go.dev/tour/welcome/1

Steps to reproduce:

1. Open https://go.dev/tour/welcome/1.
2. Focus the CodeMirror editor.
3. Press PageDown.
4. Observe that the Tour navigates to /tour/welcome/2.
5. Return to /tour/welcome/1.
6. Focus a control outside the Tour editor, for example the "Toggle theme" button in the top bar or the "A Tour of Go" logo.
7. Press PageDown again.

The same issue applies to PageUp.

I also reproduced this programmatically against the current go.dev Tour: when focus was in the CodeMirror textarea, PageDown changed /tour/welcome/1 to /tour/welcome/2; when focus was on the theme button or the Tour logo, the route remained /tour/welcome/1.

### What did you see happen?

PageUp and PageDown only navigate between Tour pages when keyboard focus is inside #editor-container or one of its descendants.

If focus moves to a focusable element outside #editor-container, such as the top-bar theme button or the "A Tour of Go" logo, pressing PageUp or PageDown no longer changes the Tour page.

This makes the documented keyboard navigation appear intermittent: it works while interacting with the lesson/editor area, but stops working after interacting with some controls in the page header.

### What did you expect to see?

PageUp and PageDown should consistently navigate to the previous or next Tour page while the user is on a Tour lesson, regardless of whether focus is currently in the editor, lesson content, or a top-bar control.

Any intentional exclusions, such as modifier-key combinations or editable controls where these keys have a specific local meaning, can still be preserved.

A custom analysis tool built with golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/singlechecker advertises and accepts -test=false, but go vet still loads and analyzes test files. The same tool honors the option when invoked directly.

Reproduced on linux/arm64 in Docker with Go built from 89066c74256e3b4891b0699c81c65a0cbd8c6844:

    go version go1.28-devel_89066c7425 Fri Sep 18 10:09:44 2026 -0700 linux/arm64

Using golang.org/x/tools v0.45.0, create these files:

```go
// vettool/main.go
package main

import (
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/printf"
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/singlechecker"
)

func main() { singlechecker.Main(printf.Analyzer) }
```

```go
// p.go
package p
```

```go
// p_test.go
package p

import "fmt"

func bad() { fmt.Printf("%d", "wrong") }
```

Then run:

```sh
go mod init example.com/repro
go get golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/singlechecker@v0.45.0
go build -o printfcheck ./vettool
go vet -vettool=./printfcheck -test=false .
```

Expected: no diagnostics from p_test.go. Actual:

```
p_test.go:5:26: fmt.Printf format %d has arg "wrong" of wrong type string
```

Invoking `./printfcheck -test=false .` succeeds without diagnostics.

The flag is discovered and forwarded by cmd/go, but cmd/go unconditionally sets ModResolveTests and calls TestPackagesFor. Singlechecker dispatches the resulting .cfg file to unitchecker, bypassing the standalone package loader that applies -test. This also means unresolved test-only imports can fail the command despite -test=false.

This was reported downstream in google/gvisor#8596 in 2023. Adin identified the driver interaction and suggested standalone invocation as a workaround. I could not find an existing Go issue for it.

A local cmd/go change applies the advertised boolean flag before package loading; a script regression fails before the change and passes after it. The flag-discovery protocol does not distinguish driver flags from analyzer flags, so treating other tools' boolean flags named test as package-selection flags is a compatibility consideration for this approach.


### What did you do?

Compared `os.Mkdir` with `Root.Mkdir` beneath a directory owned by the calling user with mode `0300` (write and search permission, but no read permission).

The standalone program below was built in the official `golang:1.26.8` Linux container and run as UID/GID `1000:1000`. The environment above is from the build step, which ran as root; the reproducer itself ran unprivileged.

Run as an unprivileged Linux user. Running with capabilities that bypass discretionary access checks can hide the problem.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "root-permission-")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)

	parent := filepath.Join(dir, "parent")
	if err := os.Mkdir(parent, 0o700); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	if err := os.Chmod(parent, 0o300); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer os.Chmod(parent, 0o700)

	root, err := os.OpenRoot(dir)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer root.Close()

	fmt.Println("os.Mkdir:", os.Mkdir(filepath.Join(parent, "ordinary"), 0o700))
	fmt.Println("Root.Mkdir:", root.Mkdir("parent/rooted", 0o700))
}
```

### What did you see happen?

```text
os.Mkdir: <nil>
Root.Mkdir: mkdirat parent/rooted: permission denied
```

The paths are entirely inside the root, with no symlinks or concurrent filesystem changes. In separate probes, ordinary stat, file creation, symlink creation, hardlink creation, chmod, and timestamp operations also succeeded beneath the same directory permissions, while their `os.Root` equivalents failed with permission denied.

This affects archive extraction using `os.Root`: a preexisting write/search-only directory, or a mode-`0300` directory created earlier in the same archive, prevents subsequent child extraction even though ordinary filesystem operations allow it.

The apparent cause is that [`rootOpenDir` opens intermediate directories without `O_PATH` or an equivalent search-only mode](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/46f508b3aa365918ac78a63340ce2343306835af/src/os/root_unix.go#L112-L129). The access mode is therefore read-only. This code is present in the tested Go 1.26.8 toolchain and in the linked upstream revision.

### What did you expect to see?

Both directory-creation operations should succeed. Creating an entry requires write and search permission on the parent, not permission to list its contents. `Root.Mkdir` should preserve these permission semantics while enforcing containment.

On Linux, a separate probe using an `O_PATH|O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW` parent descriptor followed by `mkdirat` with a single-component child name succeeded without changing directory permissions. This suggests search-only directory handles may be relevant, although a general change would need to account for other platforms and operations that actually require directory reading.

The `simd/archsimd` packages added in Go 1.26 and Go 1.27 work great for me, see also https://michael.stapelberg.ch/posts/2026-09-06-dcs-fast-turbopfor-go-simd/

I did run into one issue, though, which is that AMD Zen 4 and Zen 5 CPUs have a false dependency in their compress and expand implementation. 

The effect of this is that certain workloads, like the TurboPFor decoder I’m using in Debian Code Search, slow down significantly: consecutive expands need 4 cycles instead of 1 cycle.

LLVM has a fix for this: LLVM emits a SIMD Zeroing Idiom before compress/expand to break the false dependency. See AMD’s “Software Optimization Guide for the AMD Zen5 Microarchitecture”, section 2.9.2 for more details on zeroing idioms. See https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/206849 for the LLVM issue with more details. 

I can send a CL to make Go break the false dependency, too.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Clone https://github.com/Debian/dcs 
2. Run `make bench-baseline` in `internal/turbopfor/pfordec`
3. Undo the workaround I added:

```diff
diff --git i/internal/turbopfor/pfordec/bitunpack256vex_amd64.go w/internal/turbopfor/pfordec/bitunpack256vex_amd64.go
index 7bf24c8b..48534fda 100644
--- i/internal/turbopfor/pfordec/bitunpack256vex_amd64.go
+++ w/internal/turbopfor/pfordec/bitunpack256vex_amd64.go
@@ -130,10 +130,7 @@ func bitunpack256v32Ex(input []byte, fulloutput []uint32, nbits int, exmap *[32]
 
 // gatherExceptions loads 8 exceptions at offset j, per bitmask m.
 func gatherExceptions(exceptions *[256]uint32, j int, m byte) archsimd.Uint32x8 {
-	// VPEXPANDD has a false dependency on Zen 4 and Zen 5 (at least).
-	// Xor(zero) is a workaround; the Go compiler should do this.
-	var zero archsimd.Uint32x8
-	return archsimd.LoadUint32x8Array((*[8]uint32)(exceptions[j : j+8])).Xor(zero).Expand(archsimd.Mask32x8FromBits(m))
+	return archsimd.LoadUint32x8Array((*[8]uint32)(exceptions[j : j+8])).Expand(archsimd.Mask32x8FromBits(m))
 }
 
 func bitunpack256v32ExSIMDUnrolled[T bitWidthT](input []byte, output *[256]uint32, exmap *[32]byte, exceptions *[256]uint32) {
```

4. Run `make bench-relative` and observe how performance drops to half:

```
make -k -C \~/dcs/internal/turbopfor/pfordec/ bench-relative
make: Entering directory '/home/michael/dcs/internal/turbopfor/pfordec'
go test -pgo=decode.cpuprof
PASS
ok  	github.com/Debian/dcs/internal/turbopfor/pfordec	0.020s
taskset -c 1 go test -pgo=decode.cpuprof -run=^$ -bench=. -benchtime=200000x -count=6 | tee bench.txt
[…]
benchstat -filter '/impl:go .unit:(Mval/s)' baseline.txt bench.txt
goos: linux
goarch: amd64
pkg: github.com/Debian/dcs/internal/turbopfor/pfordec
cpu: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core Processor          
                                              │ baseline.txt │              bench.txt              │
                                              │    Mval/s    │    Mval/s     vs base               │
[…]
Decode/n=2048/vals=debian-mix/impl=go           12.121k ± 1%   6.641k ±  0%  -45.21% (p=0.002 n=6)
[…]
```

## Abstract

The FIPS140 code, especially its RNG, sits unused and bloaty on the overwhelming majority of Go binaries. All but the most specific users actually jump through the hoops of turning on this mostly useless (from a technical perspective) code. So it just sits there, wasting memory (the init functions still trigger) and wasting disk space and filling caches and just being a very unwelcome weight to a formerly clean set of crypto libraries. This proposal is to add a new `GOFIPS140=disabled` default value to not compile in unused FIPS code.

## Motivation

The new fips140 code adds lots of indirection and gravely bloats the code size of resultant binaries, even when disabled or not in use. Its use is gated by default-off GODEBUG flag. Yet it is always compiled into Go binaries.

In addition to indirecting large amounts of crypto through its framework (to then bail out early when it's not been enabled with a GODEBUG flag), it also imports large amounts of additional crypto and complexity.

As far as I can tell, in addition to causing lots of indirection through its framework, it adds branchy code paths to:

- TLS
- RSA/PKCS1
- The random number generator wrapper functions
- AES/GCM

I think adding the additional unused code is a shame in all of these cases, and all of these ought to instead be gated on a compile time constant (the `Enabled` symbol could go from `var` to `const`). But it's the RNG situation that I find especially egregious, so that's what I'll focus on here to illustrate what I mean.

I made two test programs:

tester1:
```go
package main
func main() {
        println("hello")
}
```

tester2:
```go
package main
import "crypto/rand"
func main() {
	var b [1]byte
	rand.Read(b[:])
	println("hello", b[0])
}
```

Let's see which crypto packages `tester2` adds. We'd expect that it'd pull in crypto/rand, of course, plus some internal crypto things for dispatching this to the various syscalls or whatever else involved in getting the good random bytes. That's not exactly what happens:

We get:
- A bizarre voodoo magic userspace entropy collector
- A specialized SHA384 implementation for said entropy collector
- An AES implementation
- An AES-NI accelerated AES implementation
- A CTR implementation for AES
- A GCM implementation for AES
- Some CPU detection code
- An implementation of some FIPS-specified DRBG algorithm
- An HMAC implementation
- A SHA256 implementation
- An AVX2-accelerated SHA256 implementation
- A SHA3 implementation (including cSHAKE)
- An AVX2-accelerated SHA3 implementation
- A SHA512 implementation
- Some generic XOR-bytes routines
- The actual syscall wrappers for this (crypto/internal/sysrand and crypto/rand)

This all seems a bit much to me. I mean, all of the FIPS RNG stuff seems a bit much to me, but I get that some people are forced to use it, so whatever. But that's the sort of thing that should be cordoned off into its own corner, and not _compiled in by default_ to every Go binary that uses `crypto/rand`, and especially not compiled in if it's not being used. I mean, that's a _lot_ of extra code.

## Considerations

As mentioned above, this is all gated on the GODEBUG-controlled member `fips140.Enabled`. I would suggest simply changing `fips140.Enabled` from being a `var` into being a `const`, so that the compiler can then do its usual normal thing of stripping out the unused code. Then, certain complex chains of dependencies can be fixed by using the `fips140` build tag on certain files. That would still mean that all calls get dispatched through fips140 trampolines, but at least all of the actual algorithms and excess unused code are stripped out. And the trampolines can mostly be inlined out too.

I spoke quasi-privately with @FiloSottile about this, and he expressed concern about doing this with regards to testing and CI. So part of this will involve reworking the tests so that they re-compile parts as needed. The current CL stack does this fairly cleanly.

## Proposal

So, specifically what this proposal does is proposes a new default `GOFIPS140=disabled`, which means that the binaries don't compile in any of the fips-only paths (the RNG, and the various extra branches and "silly" things). The various values are described in [this comment below](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/81639#issuecomment-5816802265), but I'll here in the proposal lay out a before and after table for the `GOFIPS140` variable:

| Value | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Unset | Defaults to `off` | Defaults to `disabled` |
| `disabled` | Invalid | FIPS mode unavailable; `fips140.Enabled` is `const false` |
| `off` | FIPS support included, disabled at startup | Same |
| `latest` | Current module, enabled by default | Same |
| `certified` | Certified snapshot, enabled by default | Same |
| `inprocess` | Snapshot undergoing certification, enabled by default | Same |
| Supported version | Specified snapshot, enabled by default | Same |

## Implementation

There's a stack of CLs available at https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/836445 and beyond that implement this, and get the testing all automated to reduce future maintenance burden.

The FIPS140 code, especially its RNG, sits unused and bloaty on the overwhelming majority of Go binaries. All but the most specific users actually jump through the hoops of turning on this mostly useless (from a technical perspective) code. So it just sits there, wasting memory (the init functions still trigger) and wasting disk space and filling caches and just being a very unwelcome weight to a formerly clean set of crypto libraries. This proposal is to add a new `GOFIPS140=disabled` default value to not compile in unused FIPS code.

## Motivation

The new fips140 code adds lots of indirection and gravely bloats the code size of resultant binaries, even when disabled or not in use. Its use is gated by default-off GODEBUG flag. Yet it is always compiled into Go binaries.

In addition to indirecting large amounts of crypto through its framework (to then bail out early when it's not been enabled with a GODEBUG flag), it also imports large amounts of additional crypto and complexity.

As far as I can tell, in addition to causing lots of indirection through its framework, it adds branchy code paths to:

- TLS
- RSA/PKCS1
- The random number generator wrapper functions
- AES/GCM

I think adding the additional unused code is a shame in all of these cases, and all of these ought to instead be gated on a compile time constant (the `Enabled` symbol could go from `var` to `const`). But it's the RNG situation that I find especially egregious, so that's what I'll focus on here to illustrate what I mean.

```go
	println("hello", b[0])
```

We get:
- A bizarre voodoo magic userspace entropy collector
- A specialized SHA384 implementation for said entropy collector
- An AES implementation
- An AES-NI accelerated AES implementation
- A CTR implementation for AES
- A GCM implementation for AES
- Some CPU detection code
- An implementation of some FIPS-specified DRBG algorithm
- An HMAC implementation
- A SHA256 implementation
- An AVX2-accelerated SHA256 implementation
- A SHA3 implementation (including cSHAKE)
- An AVX2-accelerated SHA3 implementation
- A SHA512 implementation
- Some generic XOR-bytes routines
- The actual syscall wrappers for this (crypto/internal/sysrand and crypto/rand)

This all seems a bit much to me. I mean, all of the FIPS RNG stuff seems a bit much to me, but I get that some people are forced to use it, so whatever. But that's the sort of thing that should be cordoned off into its own corner, and not _compiled in by default_ to every Go binary that uses `crypto/rand`, and especially not compiled in if it's not being used. I mean, that's a _lot_ of extra code.

## Considerations

As mentioned above, this is all gated on the GODEBUG-controlled member `fips140.Enabled`. I would suggest simply changing `fips140.Enabled` from being a `var` into being a `const`, so that the compiler can then do its usual normal thing of stripping out the unused code. Then, certain complex chains of dependencies can be fixed by using the `fips140` build tag on certain files. That would still mean that all calls get dispatched through fips140 trampolines, but at least all of the actual algorithms and excess unused code are stripped out. And the trampolines can mostly be inlined out too.

I spoke quasi-privately with @FiloSottile about this, and he expressed concern about doing this with regards to testing and CI. So part of this will involve reworking the tests so that they re-compile parts as needed. The current CL stack does this fairly cleanly.

## Proposal

So, specifically what this proposal does is proposes a new default `GOFIPS140=disabled`, which means that the binaries don't compile in any of the fips-only paths (the RNG, and the various extra branches and "silly" things). The various values are described in [this comment below](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/81639#issuecomment-5816802265), but I'll here in the proposal lay out a before and after table for the `GOFIPS140` variable:

| Value | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Unset | Defaults to `off` | Defaults to `disabled` |
| `disabled` | Invalid | FIPS mode unavailable; `fips140.Enabled` is `const false` |
| `off` | FIPS support included, disabled at startup | Same |
| `latest` | Current module, enabled by default | Same |
| `certified` | Certified snapshot, enabled by default | Same |
| `inprocess` | Snapshot undergoing certification, enabled by default | Same |
| Supported version | Specified snapshot, enabled by default | Same |

## Implementation

There's a stack of CLs available at https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/836445 and beyond that implement this, and get the testing all automated to reduce future maintenance burden.

### Go version

go version devel go1.28  darwin/arm64

### What did you do?

In an HTTP/3 server handler, called `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)` and then `w.Write([]byte("body"))`.

### What did you see happen?

`Write` returned `4, nil`. `responseWriter.Write` in `net/http/internal/http3/server.go` only rejects 304.

### What did you do?

A code generator in [CUE](https://github.com/cue-lang/cue) emits a large table of struct values, writing each field as a call to a one-line constructor such as `func cstr(v string) sval { return sval{kind: concrete, value: v} }`. Rewriting every one of those calls as the struct literal it returns — a no-op at the source level, since the constructors are trivially inlinable — took that function from 123KiB of machine code down to 52KiB, and 136KiB off the `cue` binary.

```
package main

type kind uint8

const (
	unset kind = iota
	concrete
	dflt
)

type sval struct {
	kind     kind
	value    string
	domain   []string
	excluded []string
}

// One-line constructors, of the kind a generator emits.
func cstr(v string) sval { return sval{kind: concrete, value: v} }
func dstr(v string) sval { return sval{kind: dflt, value: v} }

type entry struct {
	encoding       sval
	interpretation sval
	form           sval
}

// The two are marked noinline only so that they can be measured separately.

//go:noinline
func withCalls() *entry {
	return &entry{encoding: cstr("enc"), interpretation: dstr("interp"), form: cstr("form")}
}

//go:noinline
func withLits() *entry {
	return &entry{
		encoding:       sval{kind: concrete, value: "enc"},
		interpretation: sval{kind: dflt, value: "interp"},
		form:           sval{kind: concrete, value: "form"},
	}
}

var sink *entry

func main() {
	sink = withCalls()
	sink = withLits()
}
```

```
go build -o repro .
go tool nm -size repro | grep main.with
```

### What did you see happen?

The two functions compute the same value, but the one that goes through the constructors is almost five times as much code:

```
  47a180        533 T main.withCalls
  47a3a0        112 T main.withLits
```

The constructors are inlined, but the inlined result is not used to initialize the destination field: each `sval` is zeroed and filled in a stack temporary, and the temporary is then copied into the heap object. `withLits` writes the fields straight into the new object.

The overhead is per field, so it scales with the size of the table, which is how one generated table came to be the largest function in the `cue` binary.

### What did you expect to see?

`withCalls` and `withLits` to compile to the same code. A call whose body is a single `return T{...}` is inlined before walk, so by the time the composite literal is lowered the compiler has the field values in hand, and nothing about the semantics of the two spellings differs.

Constructor functions like these are idiomatic, and generated code leans on them heavily, so the cost is easy to pay without noticing.

### What did you see happen?

(It's somewhat easier to discover the same thing in the other direction: you can use a `UserID` as a value in a call to `DB.Query`, for example, and expect it to behave like an `int64`. But not as easy as it should be, IMO: you have to delve into the docs for the `driver` subpackage.)

When configured to use unencrypted HTTP/2 connections, the Transport can send an https:// request on an unencrypted connection:

- A Transport must be configured to not use HTTP/1 and to use both encrypted and unencrypted HTTP/2.
- An unencrypted http:// request is sent to some destination, and the unencrypted HTTP/2 connection is cached.
- A subsequent encrypted https:// request to the same destination can incorrectly use the unencrypted connection.

This is clearly a security issue, since we should never send an https:// request over an unencrypted connection.

However, the practical impact seems fairly small: Unencrypted HTTP/2 is not enabled by default and using unencrypted HTTP/2 for outgoing requests requires disabling HTTP/1 entirely. The most common use case for unencrypted HTTP/2 in the client is communicating with a server which *only* serves unencrypted HTTP/2, so sending both encrypted and unencrypted requests to the same destination is not the expected case.

As such, we're calling this a PUBLIC track issue and CVE-2026-94441.

The following is an LLM-written summary; I have not verified its validity, but it seems plausible. This issue was reported to us as a potential security bug. Image misparsing is actually the canonical example of "not every bug is a security bug" in our [security decisions](https://go.dev/doc/security/decisions#principles).

In `golang.org/x/image/vp8`, `inverseDCT4` (`vp8/idct.go`) multiplies dequantized `int16` coefficients (`z.coeff`) by `c1 = 85627` using `int32` arithmetic:

```go
c := (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+4])*c1)>>16 + (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+12])*c2)>>16
d := (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+4])*c2)>>16 - (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+12])*c1)>>16
```

When a dequantized coefficient's magnitude exceeds 25079 (math.MaxInt32 / 85627)—for example, an AC token value v = 89 with quant = 284 (base_q = 127) yielding 25276—the product int32(coeff) * c1 overflows int32 and wraps around, flipping the sign of the intermediate term and producing corrupted output pixels that diverge from libwebp (dwebp).

libwebp (TransformOne_C in src/dsp/dec.c) avoids this overflow by decomposing the multiplication as ((a * 20091) >> 16) + a (where 20091 + 65536 = 85627), or the multiplication in inverseDCT4 can be performed in int64.

The following is an LLM-written summary; I have not verified its validity, but it seems plausible. This issue was reported to us as a potential security bug. While it's clearly a bug in `webp.DecodeConfig`, we do not believe it has interesting security implications.

In `golang.org/x/image/webp`, `decode` (`webp/decode.go`, `case fccVP8X:`) returns early when `configOnly` is true (`DecodeConfig`), choosing `image.Config.ColorModel` (`color.NYCbCrAModel` or `color.YCbCrModel`) solely from the `VP8X` header's alpha flag without inspecting the subsequent image data chunk.

When `configOnly` is false (`Decode`), execution continues to the next chunk. If the image data chunk is `VP8L` (lossless WebP inside an extended `VP8X` container, such as `testdata/gopher-doc.with-alpha.lossless.webp`), `vp8l.Decode` returns an `*image.NRGBA` whose  `ColorModel()` is `color.NRGBAModel`:

```go
cfg, _ := webp.DecodeConfig(bytes.NewReader(gopherDocWithAlphaLosslessBytes))
fmt.Println(cfg.ColorModel) // color.NYCbCrAModel

img, _ := webp.Decode(bytes.NewReader(gopherDocWithAlphaLosslessBytes))
fmt.Println(img.ColorModel()) // color.NRGBAModel (*image.NRGBA)
```

As a result, DecodeConfig and Decode disagree on the ColorModel of VP8X+VP8L WebP files (and when the VP8X alpha bit is cleared on a VP8X+VP8L file, DecodeConfig reports color.YCbCrModel while Decode still returns color.NRGBAModel).

The following is an LLM-generated summary. This issue was reported to us as a potential security issue. We do not consider this to be a security but, because it requires the invoking HTTP server to pass an invalid HTTP_HOST value to the CGI program, which no reasonable server will. Probably still worth fixing as general hardening.

`cgi.RequestFromMap` (also used by `net/http/fcgi`) constructs the request URL by concatenating `HTTP_HOST` (`r.Host`) and `REQUEST_URI` (`uriStr` / `SCRIPT_NAME`) and passing the combined string `"http://" + r.Host + uriStr` to `url.Parse`:

```go
r.Host = params["HTTP_HOST"]
rawurl := r.Host + uriStr
rawurl = "http://" + rawurl
url, err := url.Parse(rawurl)
r.URL = url
```

If HTTP_HOST contains an @ character (e.g., HTTP_HOST="example.com@other.com", REQUEST_URI="/path") or if REQUEST_URI does not start with / and begins with @ (e.g., HTTP_HOST="example.com", REQUEST_URI="@other.com/path"), url.Parse interprets the prefix before @ as the URL userinfo component. This results in r.URL.Host ("other.com") diverging from r.Host.

RequestFromMap should validate r.Host / uriStr or parse the URI path separately from r.Host so that r.URL.Host cannot diverge from r.Host.

A global `sync.Pool` may contain objects, such as channels, which shouldn't cross a synctest bubble boundary. 

For example, `net/http/internal/http2` contains a pool of `chan error` which we need to skip using when inside a synctest bubble (see https://go.dev/cl/825424).

As another example, https://go.dev/cl/836565 adds a pool of channel-containing objects to `internal/poll`, and again needs to take care to skip using the pool when in a bubble.

Perhaps we should just change `sync.Pool` to skip the pool when the current goroutine is in a bubble. `Pool.Get` would always return a new object, and `Pool.Put` would be a no-op. This is always safe, and the negative impact is limited to a minor loss of performance in bubbled tests. (Tests which care about the performance characteristics of the system under test shouldn't use synctest; we don't expect bubbles to be performance-neutral.)

### Proposal Details

Add to package `maps`:

```go
// Grow increases m's capacity, if necessary, so that at least n more
// entries can be added without further growth in the typical case, as if
// m had been created with make(M, len(m)+n). Grow never shrinks m.
//
// Grow panics if n is negative. It also panics if m is nil and n > 0,
// the same as assigning to an entry in a nil map would.
func Grow[M ~map[K]V, K comparable, V any](m M, n int)
```

Split out of #56182, as requested there. Implementation: [CL 819620](https://go.dev/cl/819620).

### Motivation

`make(M, hint)` sizes a map up front, and `maps.Clone` copies one at its current size. But a map that already exists can only grow one rehash at a time. Code that merges a known number of entries into a map it doesn't own, and so can't replace, pays for every intermediate grow. In #56182, @thepudds measured presizing before a copy at 53–65% faster.

The usual idiom would be:

```go
maps.Grow(dst, len(src))
maps.Copy(dst, src)
```

### Existing code where this helps

The destination is owned by someone else in each case, so `make`/`Clone` isn't an option:

  - **net/http `TimeoutHandler`**: `maps.Copy(w.Header(), tw.h)` into the wrapped `ResponseWriter`'s header map.
    [https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7f7ce373ed87043bd9c35cfa7b0339107270b53a/src/net/http/server.go#L4218-L4219](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7f7ce373ed87043bd9c35cfa7b0339107270b53a/src/net/http/server.go#L4218-L4219)
  - **net/http/httputil `ReverseProxy`**: `copyHeader(rw.Header(), res.Header)`, called for every proxied response, plus trailers and upgrades. @jub0bs raised this case in #56182.
    [https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7f7ce373ed87043bd9c35cfa7b0339107270b53a/src/net/http/httputil/reverseproxy.go#L369-L375](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7f7ce373ed87043bd9c35cfa7b0339107270b53a/src/net/http/httputil/reverseproxy.go#L369-L375)
  - **net/http/cgi**: copies CGI response headers into `rw.Header()`.
    [https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7f7ce373ed87043bd9c35cfa7b0339107270b53a/src/net/http/cgi/host.go#L333-L337](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7f7ce373ed87043bd9c35cfa7b0339107270b53a/src/net/http/cgi/host.go#L333-L337)
  - **libhoney-go `fieldHolder.AddFields`**: this is the hand-rolled workaround. When the incoming map is larger, it allocates a new presized map, re-copies every existing entry into it, and swaps it in. Even after paying for that full re-copy, it was a net ~5% CPU saving in production. In other words, incremental growth cost more than rebuilding the whole map. `Grow` would avoid the growth without the re-copy. The other branch still grows incrementally. And the code wants in-place semantics (`Fields()` is documented to return a live reference), but it gave them up for speed: the swap silently detaches any reference a caller already holds. With `Grow`, it becomes two lines, and `Fields()` stays correct.
    [https://github.com/honeycombio/libhoney-go/blob/02e9dbf361012fafbe8698f429b65630500dc10a/libhoney.go#L642-L658](https://github.com/honeycombio/libhoney-go/blob/02e9dbf361012fafbe8698f429b65630500dc10a/libhoney.go#L642-L658) (honeycombio/libhoney-go#279)

Possible later follow-ups, not part of this proposal:

  - **`encoding/gob`** decodes into an existing non-nil map with `n` read from the stream but no presize. That would need a reflect counterpart, and `n` would need the same `saferio` bound as the `MakeMapWithSize` path (#79539).
  - **`maps.Copy`** could use `Grow` internally. Rust's `Extend` reserves the full hint for an empty map and half otherwise, for exactly this overlap reason. I'd leave `Copy` alone for now, per @CAFxX's point that heavy key overlap would over-grow.

### Prior art

  - Rust `HashMap::reserve(additional)`: same "n more" semantics.
  - .NET `Dictionary.EnsureCapacity`; C++ `unordered_map::reserve`: absolute counts.
  - OpenTelemetry Collector `pcommon.Map.EnsureCapacity`: an in-place reserve on a shared, handle-referenced map type.

### Relation to #52157

#52157 (`cap` of a map) was declined partly because map capacity "is _not_ a guarantee about being able to store that much without resizing." `Grow` doesn't expose capacity; it only takes a size hint for an existing map.

`Grow` has no return value, unlike `slices.Grow`, because the map is updated in place. That means it can't allocate a nil map; callers who have no map yet should use `make`.

`Grow` is for callers that own the map and intend to mutate it in place. When the goal is to avoid mutating a map someone else may also hold, `make` followed by `Copy` remains correct, and `Grow` doesn't replace it.

body_text:
Issue #68790 added functionality to watchflakes to watch and report broken bots. A known limitation is that it's willing to report a given unique builder at most once, but it neither reopens¹ a previous issue nor opens a new one if it happens again after some time. Currently handling issue state in those cases is handled by manually reopening/filing a new issue (for example, see the recent recurrence in https://github.com/golang/go/issues/74901#issuecomment-5798142361).

Filing this to track making watchflakes handle this automatically. @cagedmantis I couldn't find an existing tracking issue for this, but please deduplicate this if I missed something.

CC @golang/release, @thepudds.

¹ Issue #57632 may be related to the decision of whether it's better to re-open or file new issues. It may also matter how much time passed; reopening an issue so old that it's already been frozen is probably not what we want.

As reported in #81385, the tools/go/ssa package has a lot of very subtle quirks when it comes to generic methods. There now exists a lot of one off fixes when lowering functions and methods into SSA form, to handle receivers/generic type params/method exprs/etc. These fixes cause the code to become harder to understand and more brittle, as different parts of the package have to know and expect for the one off fixes without them being explicit in the type system.

We would ideally have minimal SSA specific type transformations during the lowering process, so that the SSA code is more resilient to changes upstream in the language.

body_text:
This is a follow-up to issue 1 (#81729) and only has a measurable
effect together with it.

### Go version

```
go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64
golang.org/x/crypto v0.55.0
```

### What did you do?

I called `Seal` and `Open` on the AEAD returned by `chacha20poly1305.NewX`, with the reproducer from
issue 1.

### What did you see happen?

`(*xchacha20poly1305).Seal` and `Open` derive a 32-byte subkey with `chacha20.HChaCha20`, copy it
into `c.key` of a local `chacha20poly1305` value, and return without clearing either copy. Escape
analysis inlines `HChaCha20`, and `testing.AllocsPerRun` reports 0 allocs/op for both methods, so the
subkey lives on the stack and not on the heap. It stays there until another call happens to overwrite
it.

With the fix from issue 1 applied but not this one, the reproducer still finds 16 bytes of the
subkey after both `Seal` and `Open`:

```
XChaCha20Poly1305.Seal: subkey       full=0 first16=0 last16=1
XChaCha20Poly1305.Open: subkey       full=0 first16=0 last16=1
```

### What did you expect to see?

No part of the derived subkey on the released stack.

### Proposed fix

Clear both copies of the subkey once the inner call returns:

```go
	ret := c.seal(dst, cNonce[:], plaintext, additionalData)
	clear(hKey)
	clear(c.key[:])
	return ret
```

and likewise in `Open` with `ret, err := c.open(...)`. The inner nonce `cNonce` is public and does not
need clearing.

This does not change allocations: both methods stay at 0 allocs/op, and the change is only about
the lifetime of the secret. Applied alone, without issue 1, it removes nothing measurable, because
the subkey is also held in the `state` array and in the assembly scratch area covered by issue 1.
With both changes applied, the reproducer reports zero matches (see issue 1).

body_text:
### Proposal

Add a username-aware rejection hook to `ssh.ServerConfig`:

```go
PreAuthUserCallback func(ConnMetadata) error
```

The hook runs before processing each authentication request, including the initial `none` request. Returning nil continues normal authentication. Returning an error disconnects the client with `SSH_DISCONNECT_HOST_NOT_ALLOWED_TO_CONNECT` (reason 1) and a fixed message. The application receives the error through `ServerAuthError`; its text is not sent to the client.

### Why

An SFTP server with per-user IP allowlists needs the requested username to choose the allowlist, but should reject a disallowed source address before offering password authentication. Checking in `PasswordCallback` happens after the client has already supplied a password.

`PreAuthConnCallback` runs before the username is available. `NoClientAuthCallback` requires enabling `NoClientAuth` and only handles `none` requests; clients can skip those. `BannerCallback` runs once and cannot return a rejection error. Closing a captured network connection from that callback is possible, but does not provide this per-request check and SSH disconnect response.

### Behavior and compatibility

- Leaving the hook nil preserves existing behavior. Returning nil does not authenticate anyone or change the offered methods.
- Check every request because clients can change usernames before partial authentication succeeds, repeat requests, or send credentials without a `none` probe.
- The username is a client claim, not an authenticated identity. Applications must consider whether their allow/deny responses reveal account existence.
- Expensive policy checks run before authentication and may repeat; the application remains responsible for their cost.

This proposal lets a server reject a connection before processing authentication; it does not select authentication methods. The earlier banner and multi-step-authentication proposals address different needs: #68688 and #64974.

A common mistake often (but not always) flagged during code review is to return (i.e. read from) a variable in the same statement that populates (i.e. writes to) the result variable, for example:

```go
func f(input string) (Result, err)
   var res Result
   return res, res.parse(input)
}

func (*Result) parse(string) error { ... }
```

The behavior of this program is not specified. The compiler is free to compile the load of res before or after the call to parse. The current compiler tends to make the call first, so the load observes its effect, as the code author presumably intended. But a different compiler (such as one based on x/tools/go/ssa) computes the load first, so the function always returns a zero value, even when `parse` successfully mutated the variable.

@ianlancetaylor suggested that `vet` might flag such mistakes. I did a quick experiment with a prototype analyzer (https://go.dev/cl/836485) written by a coding agent that looks for exactly the narrow pattern above. At least half, and perhaps 80%, of its findings (a sample of which are listed below) appear to be genuine bugs, so there is promise here. However, the number of false positives is too high, and the pattern is too specific, as there are undoubtedly other forms of this mistake that we could catch.

In other words, this is promising but further research is needed.

--

Here's a sample of 25 of 171 findings across 16K modules. I sampled about 10 and found 8 true bugs, and 2 that might be false positives (need closer inspection).

### Go version

go version go1.28-devel_651ec67c3b Fri Sep 25 09:02:19 2026 -0700 (master), building for `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64`. go1.27.1 generates the same code, so this isn't a regression.

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOOS=linux
GOARCH=arm64
GOARM64=v8.0
CGO_ENABLED=0
GOEXPERIMENT=
```

Cross-compiled from linux/amd64 and benchmarked on linux/arm64 (Neoverse N1).

### What did you do?

A loop multiplying by a 64-bit constant that doesn't fit an arm64 immediate, compared with the same loop loading the constant from a variable:

```go
package repro

const prime = 0xcf1bbcdcb7a56463

//go:noinline
func Hash(dst []uint32, src []uint64) {
	for i, v := range src {
		dst[i] = uint32((v * prime) >> 45)
	}
}

var primeVar uint64 = prime

//go:noinline
func HashVar(dst []uint32, src []uint64) {
	p := primeVar
	for i, v := range src {
		dst[i] = uint32((v * p) >> 45)
	}
}
```

### What did you see happen?

`Hash` rebuilds the constant with `MOVD` + 3×`MOVK` on every iteration, even though the loop uses only a handful of registers. (From `go tool objdump`, with branch targets relabelled for readability.)

```
loop:
	LSR	$45, R5, R5
	MOVW	R5, (R0)(R2<<2)
	ADD	$1, R2, R2
	CMP	R2, R4
	BLE	done
	MOVD	(R3)(R2<<3), R5
	MOVD	$25699, R6
	MOVK	$(47013<<16), R6
	MOVK	$(48348<<32), R6
	MOVK	$(53019<<48), R6
	MUL	R6, R5, R5
	CMP	R2, R1
	BHI	loop
```

`HashVar` loads it once before the loop and keeps it in `R2`:

```
	ADRP	..., R27
	MOVD	1232(R27), R2
loop:
	LSR	$45, R6, R6
	MOVW	R6, (R0)(R5<<2)
	ADD	$1, R5, R5
	CMP	R5, R4
	BLE	done
	MOVD	(R3)(R5<<3), R6
	MUL	R2, R6, R6
	CMP	R5, R1
	BHI	loop
```

On a Neoverse N1 (4096 elements, one pinned core, `-count 10`), `HashVar` is 20% faster:

```
     │   Hash    │              HashVar               │
     │  sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base               │
Hash   5.161µ ± 0%   4.128µ ± 0%  -20.02% (p=0.000 n=10)
```

For comparison, amd64 makes the same choice, rebuilding the constant inside the loop, but there it is a single `MOVQ $imm64` with no dependency chain:

```
loop:
	SHRQ	$0x2d, DX
	MOVL	DX, 0(AX)(CX*4)
	INCQ	CX
	CMPQ	SI, CX
	JLE	done
	MOVQ	0(DI)(CX*8), DX
	MOVQ	$0xcf1bbcdcb7a56463, R8
	IMULQ	R8, DX
	CMPQ	BX, CX
	JA	loop
```

so the same comparison on a Ryzen 5 5600X is much smaller:

```
     │   Hash    │              HashVar              │
     │  sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base              │
Hash   2.037µ ± 7%   1.956µ ± 2%  -3.98% (p=0.000 n=10)
```

### What did you expect to see?

The constant built once outside the loop and kept in a register, as with `HashVar`.

As far as I can tell, this is because `MOVDconst` is marked `rematerializeable: true` ([ARM64Ops.go#L413](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/651ec67c3b79c44100276c0666339c8ba1d7f727/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssa/_gen/ARM64Ops.go#L413)), and [`(*Value).Rematerializeable`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/651ec67c3b79c44100276c0666339c8ba1d7f727/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssa/regalloc.go#L165) only looks at the opcode. So the register allocator treats a constant that takes 4 instructions to build the same as one that takes 1. That's the right call on amd64, where `MOVQ $imm64` is always one instruction, but not on arm64. The `MOVDconst` ops for riscv64, ppc64, mips64 and loong64 carry the same flag. I haven't checked their code generation.

Motivation: this showed up in the zstd encoder's match-finder hashing in klauspost/compress. https://github.com/klauspost/compress/pull/1230 works around it by loading the hash primes from a package-level `var` on arm64 only (`hashPrimesInRegs = runtime.GOARCH == "arm64"`). That accounts for most of the PR's +6–8% encode throughput on Graviton2/3/4. On amd64 the same workaround is slower, because rebuilding the constant costs a single `MOVQ` and holding it adds spills in a loop that already has high register pressure. So the workaround has to be per-architecture, and it would be better fixed in the compiler.

Loop-invariant code motion (#63670) wouldn't help on its own: SSA constants already live in the entry block, outside the loop, and the register allocator re-emits them at each use.

### What did you do?

Sent a LOCK request whose `<owner>` content uses a namespace prefix declared on an ancestor element:

```xml
<d:lockinfo xmlns:d="DAV:">
  <d:lockscope><d:exclusive/></d:lockscope>
  <d:locktype><d:write/></d:locktype>
  <d:owner>
    <d:href>http://example.com</d:href>
  </d:owner>
</d:lockinfo>
```

### What did you see happen?

The `<owner>` content is echoed verbatim into a response that only declares `xmlns:D="DAV:"`, so the `d:` prefix is undefined:

```xml
<D:prop xmlns:D="DAV:"><D:lockdiscovery><D:activelock>
	...
	<D:owner>
    <d:href>http://example.com</d:href>
  </D:owner>
	...
</D:activelock></D:lockdiscovery></D:prop>
```

Namespace-aware parsers reject it, e.g. Java's XmlPullParser: `undefined prefix: d`.

`lockInfo.Owner` is decoded with `xml:",innerxml"` (xml.go), which captures raw bytes without the in-scope namespace declarations. That string becomes `LockDetails.OwnerXML` and is written unchanged by `writeLockInfo`. The existing TODO on `LockDetails.OwnerXML` in lock.go anticipates this:

> TODO: does the "verbatim" nature play well with XML namespaces?

### What did you expect to see?

A well-formed response in which every prefix inside `<D:owner>` is declared, e.g. `<d:href xmlns:d="DAV:">` or an equivalent re-encoding. A possible fix is to decode `owner` through the existing `xmlValue` type, which PROPPATCH already uses for property values. It re-encodes each token so the encoder redeclares any namespace in use.

### Go version

go version go1.26.8 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

Not relevant; reproduces with a default environment.

### What did you do?

A package declares a type whose name contains an underscore, and an example for it:

```go
// p.go
package p

type Foo_Bar struct{}
```

```go
// p_test.go
package p

import "fmt"

func ExampleFoo_Bar() {
	fmt.Println(Foo_Bar{})
	// Output: {}
}
```

Then ran `go test .`

### What did you see happen?

```
# example.com/p
# [example.com/p]
./p_test.go:5:1: ExampleFoo_Bar refers to unknown identifier: Foo
FAIL	example.com/p [build failed]
```

With `go test -vet=off .` the example builds and passes.

### What did you expect to see?

The example should be accepted, since `ExampleFoo_Bar` names the declared type `Foo_Bar`.

go/doc already resolves this case. The comment on `classifyExamples` in `src/go/doc/example.go` says:

```
//   - ExampleFoo_Bar matches a type named Foo_Bar
//     or a method named Foo.Bar.
```

and `doc.NewFromFiles` attaches `ExampleFoo_Bar` to the type `Foo_Bar`, trying each underscore as a split point. The `tests` analyzer in `checkExampleName` (`go/analysis/passes/tests/tests.go`) instead splits the name at the first underscore with `strings.SplitN(name, "_", 3)` and requires `Foo` to exist, so the two tools disagree on the same name.

Since #44251 added `tests` to the analyzers `go test` runs by default, this disagreement fails the build of any package whose exported type names contain an underscore and that has examples for them, and no configuration other than `-vet` avoids it. It would help if `checkExampleName` resolved example names the way go/doc does, accepting a name when any split matches a declared identifier.


### What did you do?

I noticed this while profiling `crypto` benchmarks. The `Keygen` benchmark in `crypto/mldsa` looked a little off in terms of memory allocation:

```
BenchmarkKeygen/ML-DSA-44-4   173323 ns/op   196608 B/op   2 allocs/op
BenchmarkKeygen/ML-DSA-65-4   267302 ns/op   196608 B/op   2 allocs/op
BenchmarkKeygen/ML-DSA-87-4   377518 ns/op   196608 B/op   2 allocs/op
```





### What did you see happen?

Extra bytes being allocated.

`crypto/mldsa` holds the internal key by value:

```
type PrivateKey struct {
        k mldsa.PrivateKey
}
```

Functions `GenerateKey` and `NewPrivateKey` return a copy like `&PrivateKey{k: *k}`, which is where the chunky bytes allocated comes from.

For refernece, `crypto/mlkem` holds its key by pointer instead:

```
type DecapsulationKey768 struct {
        key *mlkem.DecapsulationKey768
}
```

Same goes for `crypto/ecdh`, `crypto/rsa` and others.








### What did you expect to see?

I was expecting one key-sized allocation for the private key.

I made a local branch that holds a pointer instead, and I got this from benchmarks:

```
goos: linux
goarch: amd64
pkg: crypto/mldsa
cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz
                   │   old.txt   │               new.txt               │
                   │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
Keygen/ML-DSA-44-4   168.3µ ± 3%   145.8µ ± 2%  -13.39% (p=0.000 n=10)
Keygen/ML-DSA-65-4   266.9µ ± 4%   242.9µ ± 2%   -9.02% (p=0.000 n=10)
Keygen/ML-DSA-87-4   375.1µ ± 5%   353.5µ ± 4%   -5.77% (p=0.001 n=10)
geomean              256.4µ        232.2µ        -9.45%
                   │    old.txt    │               new.txt                │
                   │     B/op      │     B/op      vs base                │
Keygen/ML-DSA-44-4   192.00Ki ± 0%   96.01Ki ± 0%  -50.00% (p=0.000 n=10)
Keygen/ML-DSA-65-4   192.00Ki ± 0%   96.01Ki ± 0%  -50.00% (p=0.000 n=10)
Keygen/ML-DSA-87-4   192.00Ki ± 0%   96.01Ki ± 0%  -50.00% (p=0.000 n=10)
geomean               192.0Ki        96.01Ki       -50.00%
```

As for zero-value keys, I think some functions would have to panic (like `Bytes()`). Some can still return an error (like `Sign()`). This is somewhat related to [CL 803500](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/803500) and the discussion in #80339.

I have the branch ready for a CL. But I wanted to check first if the decision to hold the key by value is by design for some reason.

I noticed this while profiling `crypto` benchmarks. The `Keygen` benchmark in `crypto/mldsa` looked a little off in terms of memory allocation:

```
BenchmarkKeygen/ML-DSA-44-4   173323 ns/op   196608 B/op   2 allocs/op
BenchmarkKeygen/ML-DSA-65-4   267302 ns/op   196608 B/op   2 allocs/op
BenchmarkKeygen/ML-DSA-87-4   377518 ns/op   196608 B/op   2 allocs/op
```





### What did you see happen?

Extra bytes being allocated.

`crypto/mldsa` holds the internal key by value:

```
type PrivateKey struct {
        k mldsa.PrivateKey
}
```

Functions `GenerateKey` and `NewPrivateKey` return a copy like `&PrivateKey{k: *k}`, which is where the chunky bytes allocated comes from.

For refernece, `crypto/mlkem` holds its key by pointer instead:

```
type DecapsulationKey768 struct {
        key *mlkem.DecapsulationKey768
}
```

Same goes for `crypto/ecdh`, `crypto/rsa` and others.
