### What did you do?


This bug was identified by comparing floating point number conversion results across a few open-source implementations. `big.ParseFloat` and `Float.SetString` return a value one ulp off, with the wrong `Accuracy`, for decimal strings that are exactly representable or lie on or very near a halfway point. Feel free to close if this is expected/intended.

Below is the full AI-generated summary:

Parsed a few decimal strings with `big.ParseFloat` at precision 53, and compared with the exact route (`big.Rat.SetString` + `Float.SetRat`) and with `strconv.ParseFloat`. The program below is the official `golang:latest` image's go1.27.2; Go tip (`2c3c1caa`) prints the same.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"strconv"
)

func main() {
	// 2^-53, exactly representable at precision 53
	const s = "1.1102230246251565404236316680908203125e-16"
	for _, mode := range []big.RoundingMode{big.ToZero, big.ToNearestEven} {
		f, _, _ := big.ParseFloat(s, 10, 53, mode)
		fmt.Printf("ParseFloat %v: %s %v\n", mode, f.Text('p', 0), f.Acc())
	}
	r, _ := new(big.Rat).SetString(s)
	g := new(big.Float).SetPrec(53).SetMode(big.ToZero).SetRat(r)
	fmt.Printf("SetRat ToZero: %s %v\n", g.Text('p', 0), g.Acc())

	// 1 + 2^-53, the midpoint between 1 and the next float64
	a, _, _ := big.ParseFloat("1.00000000000000011102230246251565404236316680908203125", 10, 53, big.ToNearestAway)
	fmt.Printf("ParseFloat ToNearestAway: %s %v\n", a.Text('p', 0), a.Acc())

	// an 18-digit decimal near a float64 midpoint
	const t = "274497423737691809e-141"
	h, _, _ := big.ParseFloat(t, 10, 53, big.ToNearestEven)
	hf, _ := h.Float64()
	v, _ := strconv.ParseFloat(t, 64)
	fmt.Printf("big.ParseFloat:     %x\nstrconv.ParseFloat: %x\n", hf, v)
}
```


### What did you see happen?


```
ParseFloat ToZero: 0x.fffffffffffff8p-53 Below
ParseFloat ToNearestEven: 0x.8p-52 Above
SetRat ToZero: 0x.8p-52 Exact
ParseFloat ToNearestAway: 0x.8p+1 Below
big.ParseFloat:     0x1.73a056035f79fp-411
strconv.ParseFloat: 0x1.73a056035f7ap-411
```

- 2⁻⁵³ is exactly representable, but `ToZero` returns the value one ulp below it and reports `Below`. `ToNearestEven` returns the right value but reports `Above`.
- The tie 1 + 2⁻⁵³ under `ToNearestAway` gives 1 (`Below`) instead of 1 + 2⁻⁵² (`Above`).
- `274497423737691809e-141` is not a tie, just close to one. At precision 53 `ToNearestEven`, `big.ParseFloat` gives a different float64 than `strconv.ParseFloat`, and `strconv` is right.

### What did you expect to see?


The package doc says setters round "the numeric result according to the precision and rounding mode of the result variable". `Parse` "sets z to the (possibly rounded) value of the corresponding floating-point value", and `Accuracy` "describes the rounding error … relative to the exact value". So 2⁻⁵³ should parse to itself with `Exact` in every mode. The tie should follow the mode, and `274497423737691809e-141` should give `0x1.73a056035f7ap-411`. That is what `Rat.SetString` + `Float.SetRat` gives: `0x.8p-52 Exact`, `0x.80000000000008p+1 Above`, `0x.b9d02b01afbdp-410 Above`.

**Cause:** `(*Float).scan` in `src/math/big/floatconv.go` reads the mantissa exactly, then scales it by a power of 5 that is computed at only `prec+64` bits:

```go
	// apply 5**exp5
	p := new(Float).SetPrec(z.Prec() + 64) // use more bits for p -- TODO(gri) what is the right number?
	if exp5 < 0 {
		z.Quo(z, p.pow5(uint64(-exp5)))
	} else {
		z.Mul(z, p.pow5(uint64(exp5)))
	}
```

`pow5` also multiplies at `prec+64` bits (with a similar TODO). Once 5ⁿ needs more bits than that (n ≥ 51 at precision 53, n ≥ 38 at 24, n ≥ 77 at 113, n ≥ 56 at the default 64), `p` is rounded, and the quotient or product is off by roughly 2^-(prec+60). The final rounding is then correct for a slightly wrong value. That changes the result exactly when the true value is on a rounding boundary or within that error of one: exactly representable decimals (directed modes, and `Accuracy` in all modes), ties (nearest modes), and near-ties like the one above. Every precision is affected; a plain `0.000…` decimal with k fractional digits has n = −k.

**Scope:** in a differential test at precisions 2, 3, 8, 11, 24, 53, 61, 64 and 113, all five IEEE modes, and inputs concentrated on representable values and ties (normal range only), 4,626 of 65,495 parses were wrong. Of those, 1,146 were exact values moved one ulp, 766 ties went to the wrong neighbor, and 2,714 had the right value with the wrong `Accuracy`. On the 5.3 million strings of [nigeltao/parse-number-fxx-test-data](https://github.com/nigeltao/parse-number-fxx-test-data), `big.ParseFloat(s, 10, 53, ToNearestEven)` gives the wrong float64 for 5 normal-range strings, including the one above, `548994847475383618e-141`, `792644927852378159e79` (through the multiply path), and two 54-digit near-ties next to 1. `strconv.ParseFloat`, the `Rat` route and Go's own constant literals (`go/constant` keeps these as `big.Rat`) were right on everything.

A possible fix is to keep the `prec+64` fast path, but when its result is within the error bound of a rounding boundary, redo the scaling with the exact 5ⁿ (as `Rat.SetString` + `SetRat` effectively do). Computing the exact 5ⁿ every time would be expensive for inputs like `1e-1000000000`, which parse instantly today.

PKG_CONFIG='pkg-config'
```

### What did you do?

Audited `runtime/cgo` on OpenBSD/arm64.

`runtime/cgo/pthread_unix.c` calls `pthread_attr_init` but never calls `pthread_attr_destroy`. Several libcs allocate in `pthread_attr_init`, so every cgo-created thread leaks one heap object.

The non-cgo OpenBSD path in `runtime/os_openbsd.go` already destroys its attribute object.

Example:

```go
package main

/* static void noop(void) {} */
import "C"
import "runtime"

func main() {
	for range 300_000 {
		done := make(chan struct{})
		go func() {
			runtime.LockOSThread()
			C.noop()
			close(done)
		}()
		<-done
	}
}
```

Run it:

```shell
go build -o leak leak.go
(ulimit -c 0; ulimit -d 65536; ./leak)
```

### What did you see happen?

The native heap grows by about 50 bytes per retired thread. With the `ulimit` the process aborts with:

```
runtime: remapping stack memory 0x454428000 32768 a=0x0 err=12
fatal error: remapping stack memory failed
runtime: remapping stack memory 0x454480000 32768 a=0x0 err=12
fatal error: runtime: remapping stack memory 0x45440a000 32768 a=0x0 err=12
fatal error: remapping stack memory failed
remapping stack memory failed
```

### What did you expect to see?

Each successfully init'd attribute should be destroyed after `pthread_create`. In the example code, the memory usage should plateau and exit without a fault.

### What did you do?


Decoded an EXPLICIT-tagged field whose wrapper length is shorter than the element inside it.

`encoding/asn1` alone:

```go
var n int
_, err := asn1.UnmarshalWithParams([]byte{0xa0, 0x01, 0x02, 0x01, 0x01}, &n, "explicit,tag:0")
// n == 1, err == nil

A wrapper that holds more than one element moves the decoder into the wrong place: for
`struct { A int `+"`asn1:"explicit,tag:0"`"+`; B int }` and the input
`SEQUENCE { [0] { INTEGER 1, INTEGER 5 }, INTEGER 2 }` (`30 0b a0 06 02 01 01 02 01 05 02 01 02`), `Unmarshal`
returns `B == 5`, read from inside the `[0]` wrapper, and no error. A decoder that respects the wrapper length reads
`B == 2` or rejects the input.

decoded with `asn1.Unmarshal` in `getSignatureAlgorithmFromAI`. The program below creates an RSA-PSS certificate,

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/rsa"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"crypto/x509"
	"crypto/x509/pkix"
	"encoding/asn1"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"time"
)

type pair struct {
	A int `asn1:"explicit,tag:0"`
	B int
}

func main() {
	// [0] EXPLICIT wrapper with length 1 around a 3-byte INTEGER.
	var n int
	_, err := asn1.UnmarshalWithParams([]byte{0xa0, 0x01, 0x02, 0x01, 0x01}, &n, "explicit,tag:0")
	fmt.Printf("asn1: n=%d err=%v\n", n, err)

	var p pair

		SerialNumber: big.NewInt(1), Subject: pkix.Name{CommonName: "pss"},

		return
	}

	sig, _ := rsa.SignPSS(rand.Reader, key, crypto.SHA256, h[:], &rsa.PSSOptions{SaltLength: 32})

body_text:
When fetching updates for modules, the worker triggers cache invalidation. Under the hood, this executes full scan of the entire Redis keyspace. Historically this logic was added when much longer TTL was used and the Redis cache keyspaces were much smaller.

Now the redis cache has grown significantly (~700K+ keys).

Also note that the cache TTL was shortened (~10min).

As noted in [internal/worker/fetch.go#L383-L386](https://github.com/golang/pkgsite/blob/7d8a5d9065f01a262c0df4ee8d3e3e484a68091b/internal/worker/fetch.go#L383-L386), failure to invalidate cache keys is explicitly treated as low-severity:"Failure to invalidate the cache is not that serious; at worst it means some pages will be stale. (Cache TTLs for details pages configured in internal/frontend/server.go must not be too long, to account for this possibility.)"

The only user-visible effect of not actively deleting prefix keys upon fetch is that previously cached pages (such as /mod, /mod?tab=versions, or wildcard paths) may serve stale data for at most 10 minutes before expiring naturally.

Given the ratio of keyspace scanning cost to user benefit, aggressive active invalidation may be unnecessary overhead. Relying solely on Redis TTL expiry seems like a reasonable option to me.

### What version of Go are you using?

go1.25.14 (linux/amd64, official golang:1.25-bookworm image)

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes.

### What did you do?

Sent a POST request with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` where the chunk header is `5 ;x=y` — a single bad-white-space (BWS) byte between the chunk size and the semicolon that starts the chunk extension:

```python
import socket
payload = (b"POST /upload HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: t\r\nConnection: close\r\n"
           b"Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n"
           b"5 ;x=y\r\nhello\r\n0\r\n\r\n")
s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 18080)); s.sendall(payload)
print(s.recv(4096))
```

against a minimal server that reads the full body and reports framing errors:

```go
http.HandleFunc("/upload", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    body, err := io.ReadAll(r.Body)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "body framing error: "+err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "parsed-ok bytes=%d body=%q\n", len(body), body)
})
```

### What did you expect to see?

RFC 9112 §7.1.1 defines the chunk extension grammar as

```
chunk-ext = *( BWS ";" BWS chunk-ext-name [ BWS "=" BWS chunk-ext-val ] )
```

so BWS is explicitly permitted *before* the semicolon as well as after it, and the request should be accepted (as `5;x=y` and `5; x=y` both are).

### What did you see instead?

`400 Bad Request` with body `body framing error: invalid byte in chunk length` — the BWS byte is hit while still scanning the chunk-size token.

Note the asymmetry: `5; x=y` (BWS *after* the semicolon) is accepted, while `5 ;x=y` (BWS *before* it) is rejected, so BWS support is currently one-sided relative to RFC 9112 §7.1.1.

### Context

- RFC 7230 did not allow BWS here; RFC 9112 adopted the relaxation (this was also the subject of verified errata against RFC 7230).
- The rejection propagates to stacks built on net/http: Caddy v2.11.7 returns 502 for the same request, while nginx 1.31.7, Apache httpd 2.4.69, and HAProxy 3.4.7 all accept it, so the same bytes produce different outcomes across a deployment chain.
- Related: #77285 tightened chunk-extension handling in the opposite direction (CR/LF in quoted strings). If rejecting BWS before the semicolon is intentional hardening, it would help to have that documented; otherwise this looks like a conformance gap with RFC 9112 §7.1.1.

```

</details>

### What did you do?

I used a three-file module. `go.mod`:

```go
module example.com/cgoexample

go 1.26
```

`doc.go` and `helper.go` have no cgo and no build constraint:

```go
// Package cgoexample has a cgo file for a single platform.
package cgoexample
```

```go
package cgoexample

// Version reports the package version.
func Version() string {
	return "1.0.0"
}
```

`rand_darwin.go` is the only cgo file, constrained to darwin:

```go
//go:build darwin && !ios

package cgoexample

/*
#include <stdlib.h>
*/
import "C"

// Rand returns a pseudo-random number from the C library.
func Rand() int {
	return int(C.rand())
}
```

Building for the host succeeds, while a darwin build needs a C toolchain for that target:

```console
$ go build ./...
$ echo $?
0

$ GOOS=darwin CGO_ENABLED=1 go build ./...
# runtime/cgo
cgo: C compiler "clang" not found: exec: "clang": executable file not found in %PATH%
$ echo $?
1
```

`CGO_ENABLED=0` makes the darwin build succeed, which is the behaviour described for gopls views of non-default platforms:

```console
$ GOOS=darwin CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./...
$ echo $?
0
```

### What did you see happen?

Because `rand_darwin.go` is part of the package, gopls creates a darwin view for it. Loading that view fails, and the failure is attributed to every file in the package:

```console
$ gopls check -severity=warning ./doc.go ./helper.go ./rand_darwin.go
doc.go: go list failed to return CompiledGoFiles for "cgoexample"
# runtime/cgo
cgo: C compiler "clang" not found: exec: "clang": executable file not found in %PATH%
This may indicate failure to perform cgo processing; try building at the command line. See https://golang.org/issue/38990. [darwin]
helper.go: go list failed to return CompiledGoFiles for "cgoexample"
# runtime/cgo
cgo: C compiler "clang" not found: exec: "clang": executable file not found in %PATH%
This may indicate failure to perform cgo processing; try building at the command line. See https://golang.org/issue/38990. [darwin]
rand_darwin.go: go list failed to return CompiledGoFiles for "cgoexample"
# runtime/cgo
cgo: C compiler "clang" not found: exec: "clang": executable file not found in %PATH%
This may indicate failure to perform cgo processing; try building at the command line. See https://golang.org/issue/38990. [darwin]
rand_darwin.go:12:15-19: undefined: C.rand [darwin]
```

Checking the files one at a time does not show it; the darwin-constrained cgo file has to be part of the same analysis:

```console
$ gopls check -severity=warning ./helper.go
(no diagnostics)
```

`doc.go` and `helper.go` have nothing to do with cgo or with darwin, yet they carry the load failure, and the only line that points at a real location is the one in `rand_darwin.go`.

### What did you expect to see?

`gopls/doc/workspace.md` says this about views whose platform differs from the default toolchain:

> When working in a `GOOS/GOARCH` constrained file that does not match your default toolchain, `CGO_ENABLED=0` is implicitly set, since a C toolchain for that target is unlikely to be available. This means that gopls will not work in files including `import "C"`.

The failure above looks like `CGO_ENABLED` kept its ambient value of 1, so I would expect either the documented behaviour, or a diagnostic that does not implicate unrelated files.

### Editor and settings

Seen in VS Code with the Go extension: the Problems panel shows `go list failed to return CompiledGoFiles for "<pkg>"` together with the cgo error, attached to ordinary files of the package.

### Notes

The env overlay for a view created to match a build-constrained file sets only `GOOS` and `GOARCH` (`gopls/internal/cache/view.go`, in `defineView`):

```go
def.envOverlay["GOOS"] = p.GOOS
def.envOverlay["GOARCH"] = p.GOARCH
```

Searching `golang/tools` for `CGO_ENABLED`, the only non-test, non-comment hits are `internal/stdlib/generate.go` (unrelated code generation that hardcodes `GOOS=linux`), `internal/testenv/testenv.go` (a test helper), and `gopls/internal/settings/settings.go` (accepting an `int` value for a user setting). Nothing sets it implicitly for a view, and I could not find it in the commit history either. I can only describe the current code, not the original intent.

Related: #65758 tracks better support for `CGO_ENABLED=0` generally. #38990 (quoted in the message above) and #78083 are closed.

body_text:
We recently finished [BazelCon 2026](https://events.linuxfoundation.org/bazelcon/), where I spoke with several members of the Bazel community using rules_go, including engineers from Apple, Datadog, and Uber. A common concern was the resource usage of `cmd/link` when building large numbers of test binaries in their monorepos.

These repositories generally share the following characteristics:

- They are Go-dominated monorepos with tens to hundreds of thousands of test binary targets.
- Tests are built and executed using Bazel and rules_go.
- Many test targets have large, overlapping dependency closures.

### Background: rules_go

[rules_go](https://github.com/bazel-contrib/rules_go#overview) provides Bazel rules for building Go libraries, executables, and tests. Rather than delegating builds to `go build` or `go test`, it invokes the Go compiler and linker directly, while Bazel manages dependencies, scheduling, caching, and execution.

The [core rules documentation](https://github.com/bazel-contrib/rules_go/blob/master/docs/go/core/rules.md) explains the main concepts: `go_library` represents a Go package, `go_binary` produces an executable, and `go_test` produces a test executable, including the internal/external test packages and a generated test main.

### The workload

A typical `go_test` target, usually corresponding to one Go package, has a dependency graph containing package compilation actions (`GoCompilePkg`), followed by a link action (`GoLink`) that produces the test executable and a test execution action (`TestRunner`). Bazel caches and reuses package compilation outputs across targets.

The `GoLink → TestRunner` sequence is usually at the end of the build graph. Changes to transitive dependencies can invalidate these actions even when most of their inputs remain unchanged.

In practice, some teams find that test binaries have limited reuse relative to their storage and transfer costs. They therefore choose not to cache these binaries remotely, effectively producing a large executable, running it once, and then discarding it.

### Resource usage

For packages with large dependency closures, `cmd/link` must process many input archives to produce each test binary. The CPU and memory costs can be substantial, and much of this work is repeated across test binaries with common dependencies.

Bazel aggressively parallelizes independent actions. When several large `GoLink` actions run concurrently on the same machine, their combined resource usage can cause contention and, in some cases, out-of-memory kills.

This creates two related costs:

- **Repeated linker work** across test binaries that contain much of the same dependency code.
- **Producing, storing, and transferring large test executables**, even when each executable is used only once.

Caching an identical complete test binary can help with repeated executions, but it does not address the duplication between different test binaries or between versions whose inputs have changed.

We recently shipped **Content Defined Chunking (CDC)** to improve caching of these binaries over the network by allowing unchanged chunks to be reused across binary versions. This helps reduce network transfer costs, but it does not reduce the CPU or memory required by `cmd/link` to produce each binary. The linker compute cost therefore remains a separate problem.

### Possible directions

I would like to bring this workload to the Go team’s attention and ask for recommendations. Two possible approaches came up in discussions among rules_go users, but neither is intended as a prescribed solution:

1. **Incremental linking.** Reuse a previous link result and update the affected portions of the executable. One idea is to retain a mapping from input archives and symbols to output locations, together with the relocation and layout information needed for correct reuse. Changes that cannot be handled incrementally could fall back to a full link.

2. **Shared dependency images.** Factor commonly used code—such as the standard library and relatively stable third-party dependencies—out of individual test executables. These shared artifacts could have higher cache reuse than the first-party application and test code. The goal would be to reduce repeated linking and duplicated output bytes, while retaining separate test
executables and existing test semantics.

For the second approach, Bazel could ensure that the shared image and its consumers use the same toolchain, configuration, and exact dependency versions. This would not require a stable ABI across Go releases or independently updatable deployed libraries.

### Related discussions

Several earlier discussions appear relevant:

- [Building a better Go linker](https://go.dev/s/better-linker), particularly “Beyond a better linker,” discusses fast linking and execution of tests without producing short-lived executables.
- [Russ Cox’s explicit shared-image suggestion in golang/go#47788](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/47788#issuecomment-954890659) describes supplying a shared image directly to subsequent builds, avoiding installation state in `GOROOT`.
- [rules_go#4550: go_shared_library](https://github.com/bazel-contrib/rules_go/issues/4550) discusses shared libraries for this specific Bazel workload, including compatibility requirements and a possible restricted interface.
- [golang/go#77349: caching linked binaries](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/77349) discusses caching complete test executables. That seems complementary to reducing duplicated work and bytes across different executables.
- [golang/go#65226: combining tests into one binary](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/65226) discusses combining multiple packages into one test binary and the resulting semantic problems. We would prefer to preserve separate test processes rather than require that change.

### Questions

Is there a recommended direction for reducing linker resource usage and duplicated artifacts in this workload?

Would incremental linking, explicitly shared dependency images, or another form of reusable linker work be worth exploring? Are there existing efforts we should follow or contribute to?

It would also be helpful to understand which workload measurements, profiles, or representative examples would be most useful for evaluating potential improvements.

In practice, some teams find that test binaries have limited reuse relative to their storage and transfer costs. They therefore choose not to cache these binaries remotely, effectively producing a large executable, running it once, and then discarding it.

### Resource usage

For packages with large dependency closures, `cmd/link` must process many input archives to produce each test binary. The CPU and memory costs can be substantial, and much of this work is repeated across test binaries with common dependencies.

Bazel aggressively parallelizes independent actions. When several large `GoLink` actions run concurrently on the same machine, their combined resource usage can cause contention and, in some cases, out-of-memory kills.

This creates two related costs:

- **Repeated linker work** across test binaries that contain much of the same dependency code.
- **Producing, storing, and transferring large test executables**, even when each executable is used only once.

Caching an identical complete test binary can help with repeated executions, but it does not address the duplication between different test binaries or between versions whose inputs have changed.

We recently shipped **Content Defined Chunking (CDC)** to improve caching of these binaries over the network by allowing unchanged chunks to be reused across binary versions. This helps reduce network transfer costs, but it does not reduce the CPU or memory required by `cmd/link` to produce each binary. The linker compute cost therefore remains a separate problem.

### Possible directions

I would like to bring this workload to the Go team’s attention and ask for recommendations. Two possible approaches came up in discussions among rules_go users, but neither is intended as a prescribed solution:

1. **Incremental linking.** Reuse a previous link result and update the affected portions of the executable. One idea is to retain a mapping from input archives and symbols to output locations, together with the relocation and layout information needed for correct reuse. Changes that cannot be handled incrementally could fall back to a full link.

2. **Shared dependency images.** Factor commonly used code—such as the standard library and relatively stable third-party dependencies—out of individual test executables. These shared artifacts could have higher cache reuse than the first-party application and test code. The goal would be to reduce repeated linking and duplicated output bytes, while retaining separate test
executables and existing test semantics.

For the second approach, Bazel could ensure that the shared image and its consumers use the same toolchain, configuration, and exact dependency versions. This would not require a stable ABI across Go releases or independently updatable deployed libraries.

### Related discussions

Several earlier discussions appear relevant:

- [Building a better Go linker](https://go.dev/s/better-linker), particularly “Beyond a better linker,” discusses fast linking and execution of tests without producing short-lived executables.
- [Russ Cox’s explicit shared-image suggestion in golang/go#47788](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/47788#issuecomment-954890659) describes supplying a shared image directly to subsequent builds, avoiding installation state in `GOROOT`.
- [rules_go#4550: go_shared_library](https://github.com/bazel-contrib/rules_go/issues/4550) discusses shared libraries for this specific Bazel workload, including compatibility requirements and a possible restricted interface.
- [golang/go#77349: caching linked binaries](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/77349) discusses caching complete test executables. That seems complementary to reducing duplicated work and bytes across different executables.
- [golang/go#65226: combining tests into one binary](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/65226) discusses combining multiple packages into one test binary and the resulting semantic problems. We would prefer to preserve separate test processes rather than require that change.

### Questions

Is there a recommended direction for reducing linker resource usage and duplicated artifacts in this workload?

Would incremental linking, explicitly shared dependency images, or another form of reusable linker work be worth exploring? Are there existing efforts we should follow or contribute to?

It would also be helpful to understand which workload measurements, profiles, or representative examples would be most useful for evaluating potential improvements.

to appear in the parsed and re-rendered test results appearing in the luci output.

I parsed the attached CRL using `x509.ParseRevocationList`.

The `LocalityName` attribute in the issuer field has an incorrect length: its value length is set to 8, while an extra byte `0x66` remains inside the same `AttributeTypeAndValue` sequence.

Go successfully parsed the malformed CRL and completed the conversion.

```
package main

	"crypto/x509"
	"fmt"
	"os"
)

func main() {
	data, err := os.ReadFile("issuer_attribute_trailing_data.der")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	crl, err := x509.ParseRevocationList(data)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Printf("parse failed: %v\n", err)
		return
	}

	fmt.Printf("parse succeeded\n")
	fmt.Printf("issuer: %s\n", crl.Issuer.String())
}
```

`x509.ParseRevocationList` should reject the CRL because the issuer attribute contains unparsed trailing data.

body_text:
### Go version

go version go1.27.2 linux/amd64 and windows/amd64. Also reproduced with go1.23.12 and at master (dfc6f7db9b).

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOARCH='amd64'
GOOS='linux'
```

and `GOOS='windows'` for the Windows runs.

### What did you do?

One goroutine calls `ReadDir(-1)` on a directory in a loop while the main goroutine calls `Close` on the same `*os.File`. With `-seek`, the main goroutine calls `Seek(0, io.SeekStart)` instead.

<details>
<summary>Program (standard library only)</summary>

```go
// Command readdirclose calls ReadDir on a directory while another
// goroutine closes it. The os documentation says that the methods of
// File are safe for concurrent use.
package main

import (
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"runtime"
	"strconv"
	"sync"
	"sync/atomic"
)

func main() {
	seek := flag.Bool("seek", false, "call Seek instead of Close concurrently with ReadDir")
	flag.Parse()
	fmt.Println(runtime.Version(), runtime.GOOS+"/"+runtime.GOARCH)
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "readdirclose")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	for i := range 100 {
		if err := os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, strconv.Itoa(i)), nil, 0o666); err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
	}
	const trials = 100000
	for trial := 1; trial <= trials; trial++ {
		f, err := os.Open(dir)
		if err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
		var wg sync.WaitGroup
		wg.Add(1)
		var stop atomic.Bool
		go func() {
			defer wg.Done()
			for !stop.Load() {
				if _, err := f.ReadDir(-1); err != nil {
					return // f has been closed
				}
			}
		}()
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\rtrial %d", trial)
		if *seek {
			for range 100 {
				f.Seek(0, io.SeekStart)
			}
			stop.Store(true)
			wg.Wait()
			f.Close()
		} else {
			f.Close()
			wg.Wait()
		}
	}
	fmt.Printf("\nno crash in %d trials\n", trials)
}
```

</details>

### What did you see happen?

The process crashes in `os.(*File).readdir`:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x10 pc=0x4a1240]

goroutine 1194 [running]:
os.(*File).readdir(0x1ada97602048, 0xffffffffffffffff, 0x1)
	src/os/dir_unix.go:100 +0x2a0
os.(*File).ReadDir(0x0?, 0x0?)
	src/os/dir.go:101 +0x1d
main.main.func1()
	main.go:44 +0x72
```

| Go | GOOS | crashed at trial | in |
|---|---|---:|---|
| master (dfc6f7db9b) | linux | 824 | dir_unix.go:86 |
| go1.27.2 | linux | 1472 | dir_unix.go:100 |
| go1.23.12 | linux | 1604 | dir_unix.go:92 |
| master (dfc6f7db9b) | windows | 87 | dir_windows.go:165 |
| go1.27.2 | windows | 236 | dir_windows.go:165 |
| go1.23.12 | windows | 62 | dir_windows.go:165 |

On Windows the signal is `0xc0000005`. With `-seek`, at master on linux, it crashed at trial 35 in dir_unix.go:100. Under `-race`, at master on linux:

```
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c0000de3a8 by goroutine 46:
  os.(*File).readdir()
      src/os/dir_unix.go:65 +0x1dd
  os.(*File).ReadDir()
      src/os/dir.go:101 +0x3e
  main.main.func1()
      main.go:44 +0xaa

Previous read at 0x00c0000de3a8 by main goroutine:
  os.(*dirInfo).close()
      src/os/dir_unix.go:41 +0x5d
  os.(*file).close()
      src/os/file_unix.go:312 +0x58
  os.(*File).Close()
      src/os/file_posix.go:24 +0x594
  main.main()
      main.go:58 +0x595
```

`(*file).close` (file_unix.go:311-313, file_windows.go:175-177) and `(*File).seek` (file_unix.go:332-336, file_windows.go:196-200) take the `dirInfo` out of the File with `Swap(nil)` and call `(*dirInfo).close`. That returns `d.buf` to `dirBufPool` and sets it to nil without holding `d.mu` (dir_unix.go:40-45, dir_windows.go:49-55). A `readdir` that loaded the same `dirInfo` before the swap holds `d.mu` and goes on using `d.buf` (for example dir_unix.go:86 and dir_windows.go:125), so it dereferences nil, or uses a buffer that is already back in the pool.

On darwin, `dirInfo` has no mutex, and `(*dirInfo).close` calls `closedir` (dir_darwin.go:20-26) while `readdir` may be using the same `DIR` in `readdir_r` (dir_darwin.go:57). I have not run this on darwin.

### What did you expect to see?

`ReadDir` returning an error once the File is closed, and no crash for `Seek`. The `os` documentation says "The methods of File are safe for concurrent use" (types.go:17). That sentence came with [CL 578322](https://go.dev/cl/578322) for #66498, which made the ReadDir methods safe against each other. #66498 also included a report of this crash with `Readdirnames` and `Close` ([https://github.com/golang/go/issues/66498#issuecomment-2033462093](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/66498#issuecomment-2033462093)). The Close and Seek paths still release the buffer without taking the lock.

go version go1.27.2 linux/amd64 and windows/amd64. Also reproduced with go1.23.12 and at master (dfc6f7db9b).

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOARCH='amd64'
GOOS='linux'
```

and `GOOS='windows'` for the Windows runs.

### What did you do?

One goroutine calls `ReadDir(-1)` on a directory in a loop while the main goroutine calls `Close` on the same `*os.File`. With `-seek`, the main goroutine calls `Seek(0, io.SeekStart)` instead.

<details>
<summary>Program (standard library only)</summary>

```go
// Command readdirclose calls ReadDir on a directory while another
// goroutine closes it. The os documentation says that the methods of
// File are safe for concurrent use.
package main

import (
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"runtime"
	"strconv"
	"sync"
	"sync/atomic"
)

func main() {
	seek := flag.Bool("seek", false, "call Seek instead of Close concurrently with ReadDir")
	flag.Parse()
	fmt.Println(runtime.Version(), runtime.GOOS+"/"+runtime.GOARCH)
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "readdirclose")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	for i := range 100 {
		if err := os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, strconv.Itoa(i)), nil, 0o666); err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
	}
	const trials = 100000
	for trial := 1; trial <= trials; trial++ {
		f, err := os.Open(dir)
		if err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
		var wg sync.WaitGroup
		wg.Add(1)
		var stop atomic.Bool
		go func() {
			defer wg.Done()
			for !stop.Load() {
				if _, err := f.ReadDir(-1); err != nil {
					return // f has been closed
				}
			}
		}()
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\rtrial %d", trial)
		if *seek {
			for range 100 {
				f.Seek(0, io.SeekStart)
			}
			stop.Store(true)
			wg.Wait()
			f.Close()
		} else {
			f.Close()
			wg.Wait()
		}
	}
	fmt.Printf("\nno crash in %d trials\n", trials)
}
```

</details>

### What did you see happen?

The process crashes in `os.(*File).readdir`:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x10 pc=0x4a1240]

goroutine 1194 [running]:
os.(*File).readdir(0x1ada97602048, 0xffffffffffffffff, 0x1)
	src/os/dir_unix.go:100 +0x2a0
os.(*File).ReadDir(0x0?, 0x0?)
	src/os/dir.go:101 +0x1d
main.main.func1()
	main.go:44 +0x72
```

| Go | GOOS | crashed at trial | in |
|---|---|---:|---|
| master (dfc6f7db9b) | linux | 824 | dir_unix.go:86 |
| go1.27.2 | linux | 1472 | dir_unix.go:100 |
| go1.23.12 | linux | 1604 | dir_unix.go:92 |
| master (dfc6f7db9b) | windows | 87 | dir_windows.go:165 |
| go1.27.2 | windows | 236 | dir_windows.go:165 |
| go1.23.12 | windows | 62 | dir_windows.go:165 |

On Windows the signal is `0xc0000005`. With `-seek`, at master on linux, it crashed at trial 35 in dir_unix.go:100. Under `-race`, at master on linux:

```
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c0000de3a8 by goroutine 46:
  os.(*File).readdir()
      src/os/dir_unix.go:65 +0x1dd
  os.(*File).ReadDir()
      src/os/dir.go:101 +0x3e
  main.main.func1()
      main.go:44 +0xaa

Previous read at 0x00c0000de3a8 by main goroutine:
  os.(*dirInfo).close()
      src/os/dir_unix.go:41 +0x5d
  os.(*file).close()
      src/os/file_unix.go:312 +0x58
  os.(*File).Close()
      src/os/file_posix.go:24 +0x594
  main.main()
      main.go:58 +0x595
```

`(*file).close` (file_unix.go:311-313, file_windows.go:175-177) and `(*File).seek` (file_unix.go:332-336, file_windows.go:196-200) take the `dirInfo` out of the File with `Swap(nil)` and call `(*dirInfo).close`. That returns `d.buf` to `dirBufPool` and sets it to nil without holding `d.mu` (dir_unix.go:40-45, dir_windows.go:49-55). A `readdir` that loaded the same `dirInfo` before the swap holds `d.mu` and goes on using `d.buf` (for example dir_unix.go:86 and dir_windows.go:125), so it dereferences nil, or uses a buffer that is already back in the pool.

On darwin, `dirInfo` has no mutex, and `(*dirInfo).close` calls `closedir` (dir_darwin.go:20-26) while `readdir` may be using the same `DIR` in `readdir_r` (dir_darwin.go:57). I have not run this on darwin.

### What did you expect to see?

`ReadDir` returning an error once the File is closed, and no crash for `Seek`. The `os` documentation says "The methods of File are safe for concurrent use" (types.go:17). That sentence came with [CL 578322](https://go.dev/cl/578322) for #66498, which made the ReadDir methods safe against each other. #66498 also included a report of this crash with `Readdirnames` and `Close` ([https://github.com/golang/go/issues/66498#issuecomment-2033462093](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/66498#issuecomment-2033462093)). The Close and Seek paths still release the buffer without taking the lock.

@chrisddwrt requested issue #80288 to be considered for backport to the next 1.26 minor release.
> Independent confirmation on real hardware, plus a request to backport the fix to the supported release branches.
>
> **Reproduced** with the program below on amd64 hardware (Intel Xeon, AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ) with go1.24.7 and go1.25.1, and on arm64 hardware (Apple M-series, AES+PMULL) with go1.24.7 and go1.25.1 under Linux 6.8 and with go1.26.3 under macOS — identical results everywhere. release-branch.go1.25 (go1.25.14) and release-branch.go1.26 (go1.26.9) still contain the unfixed assembly (checked in git, not run). The arm64 path is the same construction (`gcm_arm64.s`, `encReduce:` → `VST1.P [B0.B16], 16(dstPtr)` reached from `tailLast:`). With `-tags purego` nothing is written out of bounds.
>
> Exact behaviour on all affected versions (guard bytes behind a destination slice of exact capacity):
>
> | tag size | plaintext length (mod 16) | bytes written past cap(dst) |
> |---|---|---|
> | 12 | 1 / 2 / 3 | 3 / 2 / 1 |
> | 13 | 1 / 2 | 2 / 1 |
> | 14 | 1 | 1 |
> | 15, 16 | – | none |
>
> i.e. `16 - (len % 16) - tagSize` when positive. The bytes written are always zero (the block is masked with `andMask` before the full-block store at `gcm_amd64.s` `ptxLoadLoop` → `MOVOU X0, (DX)`). Plaintexts shorter than one block (len 1..3) are affected too. `Open` only over-reads up to 3 bytes.
>
> **Why "nearly always harmless due to allocator semantics" does not hold in practice:** the slack argument assumes `dst` is a freshly allocated slice whose size class leaves padding. In packet-processing code `dst` is routinely a sub-slice of a larger live buffer — `buf[:0:n]`, ring buffers, `sync.Pool` buffers, send buffers that already hold the next packet. We hit this in production code: the zero bytes landed in a pooled HMAC state (`crypto/sha256: invalid hash state identifier`) and, on go1.24, in a SIGSEGV. Any program using `NewGCMWithTagSize` with 12–14 byte tags on amd64/arm64 with hardware AES can be affected, and the plaintext length is attacker-controlled in most network protocols.
>
> The fix ([CL 801600](https://go.dev/cl/801600), e36c20c7a) is currently only on master. Since this is a memory-safety bug in `crypto/cipher` with an attacker-influenceable trigger, and the fix is small and self-contained (tail load/store only, with new boundary tests), could it please be considered for backport to go1.25 and go1.26?
>
> @gopherbot please consider this for backport to 1.25 and 1.26: memory safety issue in crypto/cipher (out-of-bounds write with short GCM tags), fix is on master.
>
> Minimal reproduction (prints the number of bytes written past cap for each length):
>
> ```go
> package main
> 
> import (
> 	"crypto/aes"
> 	"crypto/cipher"
> 	"fmt"
> 	"runtime"
> )
> 
> func main() {
> 	blk, _ := aes.NewCipher(make([]byte, 16))
> 	a, _ := cipher.NewGCMWithTagSize(blk, 12)
> 	nonce := make([]byte, 12)
> 	for _, l := range []int{1, 17, 18, 19, 20, 33} {
> 		buf := make([]byte, l+12+8)
> 		for i := range buf {
> 			buf[i] = 0xEE
> 		}
> 		a.Seal(buf[:0:l+12], nonce, make([]byte, l), nil) // dst has exact capacity
> 		over := 0
> 		for _, c := range buf[l+12:] {
> 			if c != 0xEE {
> 				over++
> 			}
> 		}
> 		fmt.Printf("%s %s len=%d: %d bytes written past cap(dst)\n", runtime.Version(), runtime.GOARCH, l, over)
> 	}
> }
> ```

### Go version

go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell

GOVERSION='go1.27.0'
GOWORK=''
PKG_CONFIG='pkg-config'
```

### What did you do?

A benchmark that panics with a value whose `Error` method is slow. The runtime calls that method to print the panic before it ends the process, which widens the window this bug needs, so the result is deterministic:

```go
// repro_test.go, in a module with `go 1.26`
package repro

import (
	"testing"
	"time"
)

type slowErr struct{}

func (slowErr) Error() string {
	time.Sleep(time.Second)
	return "boom"
}

func BenchmarkPanic(b *testing.B) {
	panic(slowErr{})
}
```

```shell
go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchtime=1x -count=1 .
```

The same happens without the slow `Error` method, only rarely. A benchmark whose body is just `panic("boom")` loses the panic about 1 run in 200 on a busy machine. This loop runs its compiled test binary 2000 times, eight at a time, and prints how many runs exited 0 (it should print 0):

```shell
go test -c -o repro.test .
for j in $(seq 1 8); do
  ( for i in $(seq 1 250); do
      ./repro.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime=1x >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "exit 0"
    done ) &
done | wc -l
wait
```

### What did you see happen?

With the slow `Error` method, every run reports the benchmark as passing. The panic is never printed:

```
goos: linux
goarch: amd64
pkg: repro
cpu: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D 16-Core Processor
BenchmarkPanic-6   	       1
PASS
ok  	repro	0.004s
```

The test binary run directly exits 0 in 10 of 10 runs, on go1.27.0 and go1.26.9 alike.

With `panic("boom")`, most runs panic and exit 2 as expected, but some print the same `PASS` and exit 0:

| Program | go1.27.0 | go1.26.9 |
|---|---|---|
| test binary, 2000 runs | 10 exited 0 | 10 exited 0 |
| `go test -bench`, 480 runs (go1.27.0) | 3 reported `ok` | |

The panic is lost wherever it happens on the benchmark's goroutine. I measured 1600 runs each on go1.27.0 for:

- a panic in a `b.Cleanup` function of a benchmark with a sub-benchmark: 8 exited 0;
- a panic in the benchmark body after a sub-benchmark ran: 8 exited 0;
- a panic in a sub-benchmark's body: 5 exited 0.

We first saw it as an intermittent CI failure on `windows-latest` (GitHub Actions): a benchmark whose cleanup panics printed `PASS` and exited 0.

### What did you expect to see?

Every run should end with the panic and its traceback, a non-zero exit status, and `FAIL` from the go command, as a panicking test does. A benchmark that panics must never be reported as passing.

What seems to happen: `(*B).run1` (and likewise `(*B).launch`) runs the benchmark on a new goroutine whose deferred function sends on `b.signal`. The comment there says this is so that a return through `FailNow`'s `runtime.Goexit` also signals. But deferred functions also run while a panic unwinds, so a panic signals the benchmark done too. ### Go version

go version go1.22.6 windows/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOOS=windows
GOARCH=amd64
GOTOOLCHAIN=auto
```

### What did you do?

Took a CPU profile on Windows Server 2019 (OS Version 10.0.17763 Build 17763, bare-metal Supermicro server), either via net/http/pprof /debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 or with runtime/pprof.StartCPUProfile in a standalone program:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"runtime/pprof"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	f, _ := os.Create("cpu.pb.gz")
	pprof.StartCPUProfile(f)
	deadline := time.Now().Add(5 * time.Second)
	x := 0
	for time.Now().Before(deadline) {
		x += x*x + 1
	}
	pprof.StopCPUProfile()
	f.Close()
	fmt.Println(x)
}
```
```
> go run main.go; go tool pprof -top cpu.pb.gz
Duration: 5s, Total samples = 0
```

For the 30 second net/http/pprof profile, `go tool pprof -raw` shows a well-formed profile with `Duration: 30.0`, all mappings present, and an empty `Samples:` section. The same binaries produce normal profiles on Windows 10 22H2 (build 19045).

Reproduced with go1.22.6 and go1.24.0 on windows/amd64. The affected code in src/runtime/os_windows.go is unchanged in go1.27.1 and on master.

### What did you see happen?

Zero samples in every CPU profile, for every Go binary, on this Windows build. No error or warning is printed.

### What did you expect to see?

CPU samples, as on other Windows versions.

**Root cause**

`runtime.initHighResTimer` sets `haveHighResTimer = true` when
`CreateWaitableTimerExW(CREATE_WAITABLE_TIMER_HIGH_RESOLUTION)` succeeds.
`setProcessCPUProfiler` then creates the profiler timer as a high-resolution
timer, and `setThreadCPUProfiler` arms it with a **period** via
`SetWaitableTimer(timer, &due, ms, ...)`, ignoring the return value.

On Windows 10 1803/1809 (and Server 2019, which is 1809) the high-resolution
flag is accepted at creation time, but `SetWaitableTimer` with a nonzero
`lPeriod` on such a timer fails with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` (87). The timer
is therefore never armed, `profileLoop` blocks forever in
`WaitForSingleObject(profiletimer, INFINITE)`, and no sample is ever taken.
Non-periodic use (`usleep`, period 0) works on the same build, which is why
everything else in the runtime behaves normally.

Direct Win32 reproduction on the affected machine (Go program calling kernel32
via syscall), compared with Windows 10 22H2:

```
Windows Server 2019 (17763):
  high-res timer: SetWaitableTimer failed: The parameter is incorrect.
  normal timer  : 100 fires in 1 s (expect ~100)
  SuspendThread -> 0, GetThreadContext -> 1, ResumeThread -> 1

Windows 10 22H2 (19045):
  high-res timer: 96 fires in 1 s (expect ~100)
  normal timer  : 64 fires in 1 s (expect ~100)
```

`SuspendThread`/`GetThreadContext` work, so the sampling side is fine; only the
periodic high-resolution timer is broken on this build.

**Fix**

In `setProcessCPUProfiler`, after creating the high-resolution timer, probe it
with a periodic `SetWaitableTimer`. If that fails, close it and fall back to a
regular waitable timer from `CreateWaitableTimerA`, which supports periods on
every Windows version. `setThreadCPUProfiler` is unchanged. Verified on the
affected Server 2019 machine: profiles go from 0 samples to normal coverage.
Also verified with the fallback forced on Windows 10 22H2: profiling still
works (at the coarser 15.6 ms default timer resolution, 62% coverage of a
3 s busy loop, versus ~90% with the high-resolution timer).

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOOS=windows
GOARCH=amd64
GOTOOLCHAIN=auto
```

### What did you do?

Took a CPU profile on Windows Server 2019 (OS Version 10.0.17763 Build 17763, bare-metal Supermicro server), either via net/http/pprof /debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 or with runtime/pprof.StartCPUProfile in a standalone program:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"runtime/pprof"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	f, _ := os.Create("cpu.pb.gz")
	pprof.StartCPUProfile(f)
	deadline := time.Now().Add(5 * time.Second)
	x := 0
	for time.Now().Before(deadline) {
		x += x*x + 1
	}
	pprof.StopCPUProfile()
	f.Close()
	fmt.Println(x)
}
```
```
> go run main.go; go tool pprof -top cpu.pb.gz
Duration: 5s, Total samples = 0
```

For the 30 second net/http/pprof profile, `go tool pprof -raw` shows a well-formed profile with `Duration: 30.0`, all mappings present, and an empty `Samples:` section. The same binaries produce normal profiles on Windows 10 22H2 (build 19045).

Reproduced with go1.22.6 and go1.24.0 on windows/amd64. The affected code in src/runtime/os_windows.go is unchanged in go1.27.1 and on master.

### What did you see happen?

Zero samples in every CPU profile, for every Go binary, on this Windows build. No error or warning is printed.

### What did you expect to see?

CPU samples, as on other Windows versions.

**Root cause**

`runtime.initHighResTimer` sets `haveHighResTimer = true` when
`CreateWaitableTimerExW(CREATE_WAITABLE_TIMER_HIGH_RESOLUTION)` succeeds.
`setProcessCPUProfiler` then creates the profiler timer as a high-resolution
timer, and `setThreadCPUProfiler` arms it with a **period** via
`SetWaitableTimer(timer, &due, ms, ...)`, ignoring the return value.

On Windows 10 1803/1809 (and Server 2019, which is 1809) the high-resolution
flag is accepted at creation time, but `SetWaitableTimer` with a nonzero
`lPeriod` on such a timer fails with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` (87). The timer
is therefore never armed, `profileLoop` blocks forever in
`WaitForSingleObject(profiletimer, INFINITE)`, and no sample is ever taken.
Non-periodic use (`usleep`, period 0) works on the same build, which is why
everything else in the runtime behaves normally.

Direct Win32 reproduction on the affected machine (Go program calling kernel32
via syscall), compared with Windows 10 22H2:

```
Windows Server 2019 (17763):
  high-res timer: SetWaitableTimer failed: The parameter is incorrect.
  normal timer  : 100 fires in 1 s (expect ~100)
  SuspendThread -> 0, GetThreadContext -> 1, ResumeThread -> 1

Windows 10 22H2 (19045):
  high-res timer: 96 fires in 1 s (expect ~100)
  normal timer  : 64 fires in 1 s (expect ~100)
```

`SuspendThread`/`GetThreadContext` work, so the sampling side is fine; only the
periodic high-resolution timer is broken on this build.

**Fix**

In `setProcessCPUProfiler`, after creating the high-resolution timer, probe it
with a periodic `SetWaitableTimer`. If that fails, close it and fall back to a
regular waitable timer from `CreateWaitableTimerA`, which supports periods on
every Windows version. `setThreadCPUProfiler` is unchanged. Verified on the
affected Server 2019 machine: profiles go from 0 samples to normal coverage.
Also verified with the fallback forced on Windows 10 22H2: profiling still
works (at the coarser 15.6 ms default timer resolution, 62% coverage of a
